name: The Christian walk
about: Separation, service, and walking with God.

teachings.title: Patience with the weak as God with us
teachings.summary: Bearing with weak and burdensome people is hard, but it shows how much more patience God has with all of us.
teachings.text:
Being like-minded with God in showing patience and consolation, especially to those weaker than ourselves in the faith, in general standards, in sin, intelligence, physically.... It's a struggle.

With those who become a burden, incapable of helping themselves, entitled and unwilling, who rebuff reproach, it becomes so difficult. But in it there's a lesson for those of us willing to see, how much worse it must be for God dealing with us.

Even the most spiritually minded of us try God's patience. Even those who stay in God's word daily in constant prayer, not forsaking the assembly, and winning souls to Christ, (there are very few this upright, and it certainly isn't me), try God's patience.

teachings.title: The cross I take up daily
teachings.summary: Giving up the old carnal life comes easily by the Spirit; the real cross is living for God and loving others with the patience He shows us.
teachings.text:
The turning from sin and giving up worldly pleasures and habits is actually the easiest part. With the spirit and willingness, we naturally become repulsed by the weakness of the old man of the flesh. Free of guilt and resentment, and with discernment that comes with devotion to the spiritual, it's almost nothing to go cold turkey from our carnal life.

Living for God, and loving others as ourselves, magnifying the patience and love He has shown us, that's the challenge. That's the cross I take up daily. Having faith that this will be to the glory and benefit of God, even if it costs us today, that's hard.

Paul's exhortation to do this, (and the listing of the saints who have, immortalized in Romans 16), is a sobering reminder of our shared calling in Christ.

teachings.title: Charity, the more excellent way
teachings.summary: Above every spiritual gift stands charity, the selfless unfeigned love that reflects God's love in Christ, and works done for selfish ends, above all to earn salvation, are uncharitable.
teachings.text:
Paul's more excellent way, as promised in chapter 12; charity.

That regardless of the spiritual gifts we all have, or the special gift of the Holy Ghost some in those days were blessed with, it is the unfeigned love, given for no personal gain, but genuine and selfless, that is above all else, and is a faint reflection of the love God showed us by giving His Son that we may be saved, and the love Jesus showed us while we were still sinners, to give His life for us, and taste death and Hell for our transgressions.

We usually use the basic definition of charity to mean giving something away to help others, alms. And that certainly can be a form of expression for charity, but it is not itself charity as we see in verse 3.

Paul defines it by what it's not or what qualities it has. And its qualities are those of the love, the charity of God shown towards us, that Jesus teaches us in His sermons.

So many do so much as a form of "charity" but for selfish purpose, or taking pride or accolades for it. Storing up hay and stubble without ever gaining rewards for it, because they do it in the wrong Spirit.

IMO, works done to "earn" or keep salvation being the most selfish of all, and the least charitable.

This chapter also parallels with James 2, and the "faith without works is dead, being alone" lesson. It's the true meaning. We may have faith enough to move mountains, as Paul says here, but if we have not charity it profits no one.

When the Kingdom is here and established in Christ's reign, and then when we know all things and are as an adult to a child, the mysteries all solved, charity will remain, even as all our other things we placed importance in fade.

teachings.title: Charity is the motive, not the gift
teachings.summary: Read with chapter 12, charity means caring for each member of the church and not coveting others' gifts, since tongues or knowledge without love profits nothing.
teachings.text:
We need to read the Bible in full context. Chapters and verses are there to make navigation of the word easier, but these are not stand alone concepts, but entire thoughts that span entire books.

If we look back at chapter 12, we see how Paul is leading to the lesson of charity:

*That there should be no schism in the body; but that the members should have the same care one for another. And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it.*

*Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular. And God hath set some in the church, first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers, after that miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, diversities of tongues.*

*Are all apostles? are all prophets? are all teachers? are all workers of miracles?*

*Have all the gifts of healing? do all speak with tongues? do all interpret? But covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way*

You see the charity is caring for the others in the church, sorrow for each members' sorrow, and joy for their individual success. Not coveting the gifts each may have. Edifying one another.

In Chapter 14 we will see that it is the gift of tongues driving much of the contention here, given its prominence in Paul's epistle. Thus if someone preaches in tongues, even with the language of angels, they become as sounding brass and tinkling cymbals, it's useless without charity.

We can know all things in scripture, and all knowledge can be show us, and of we aren't edifying others and given to love people, it's for nothing. It's the motive not the gift.

teachings.title: Faith, hope and charity abide
teachings.summary: Tongues, prophecy and knowledge fade away, but faith, hope and charity endure into the kingdom of God.
teachings.text:
Now, as to what abides and what fadeth away, we see it is our faith, *the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen,* our hope, a well founded expectation of good that comes from faith, the expression of that trust and belief, and charity, the unconditional love that is God's love, magnified through us, that cares for others and seeks to build them up, even at our own expense. These are what endure in the Kingdom of God.

Not tongues, various languages or soaring rhetoric, not preaching and prophecy, that fails and fades. Not knowledge, that is imperfect at best in our current state, seeing through the glass darkly. In the end, these gifts may have been blessings for the holder, and may have fed others faith, given them hope and built them up in charity, but they aren't in themselves eternal the way faith, hope and charity are.

teachings.title: Liberality to brethren in need
teachings.summary: Those who have are to share with brethren who lack, and such generosity is rewarded with spiritual abundance, reflecting the charity God shows us.
teachings.text:
Now, having established no need for letters of commendation for Titus and the brethren that accompanied him, but the shared spirit and kinship in Christ, Paul actually gives his commendation, their bona fides.

The purpose remains instruction, but specifically the gathering of the alms to bring to the church in Jerusalem, then stricken with a famine as described in Acts.

There is doctrine here, that we who have are expected to share with brethren who lack, because worldly things being unimportant, and the blessings given by God to those that do without for others, our liberality, our generosity of materials leads to our receiving abundance of the spiritual. It's an even trade, not a burden.

This is a reflection of the charity God shows us in His mercy and loving kindness. We lack, and He has abundance, and in His grace, sharing it with us, He loses nothing but gains. In the same manner, when we do the same among men we are rewarded.

teachings.title: Whosoever will be great shall be servant of all
teachings.summary: True greatness is in humbly serving others as Christ, who came to minister and promises to serve His faithful servants at His return.
teachings.text:
Finally, we see the bitter rivalry and divisions among the Apostles continued, even after Jesus taught them that the first shall be last, and the last first, that great are those in the Kingdom of Heaven who abased themselves to serve others here on Earth.

*And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, come unto him, saying, Master, we would that thou shouldest do for us whatsoever we shall desire.*

*And he said unto them, What would ye that I should do for you? They said unto him, Grant unto us that we may sit, one on thy right hand, and the other on thy left hand, in thy glory. But Jesus said unto them, Ye know not what ye ask: can ye drink of the cup that I drink of? and be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with?*

*And they said unto him, We can. And Jesus said unto them, Ye shall indeed drink of the cup that I drink of; and with the baptism that I am baptized withal shall ye be baptized: But to sit on my right hand and on my left hand is not mine to give; but it shall be given to them for whom it is prepared.*

*And when the ten heard it, they began to be much displeased with James and John. But Jesus called them to him, and saith unto them, Ye know that they which are accounted to rule over the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; and their great ones exercise authority upon them.*

*But so shall it not be among you: but whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister: And whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all. For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.*

We know from scripture James was martyred for the Gospel, baptized with the same as Jesus, drinking that same cup, while as a mercy perhaps to their mother (**Matthew 20**), spared John the fate of all His Apostles, and allowed him to die of old age, the author of much of the New Testament.

But regardless of their design on greatness in Heaven, on earth this brought even more contentiousness among the disciples. Jesus again takes the opportunity to explain that it is not about being lifted up in greatness like the rulers of this world, who are served by many, but being a lowly servant to many. Just as He, the Son of God was for us, a sacrifice.

And more, Jesus promises us, as good and trusty servants, that in His return He will again serve us;

*Blessed are those servants, whom the lord when he cometh shall find watching: verily I say unto you, that he shall gird himself, and make them to sit down to meat, and will come forth and serve them.*

What a blessing. What a God who so loves us. And if He, without sin, who cannot lie, who is Holy and True, the King of Kings, Lord of all, can humble Himself to serve us, how can we do anything less to those we meet every day? With meekness and grace, we are called to be in service to others, in Christ's name, just as He has for us.

And the last shall be first. Amen.

teachings.title: What shall we do: fruits meet for repentance
teachings.summary: John's answers to the people, publicans and soldiers show how the saved live out love thy neighbour: be honest, do not defraud or abuse your position, and be a light at work and home.
teachings.text:
Just a real quick application to today's study on **Luke 3**, something I didn't really get into this morning, but is very important.

**Luke 3:9-14**
*And now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees: every tree therefore which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire. And the people asked him, saying, What shall we do then? He answereth and saith unto them, He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do likewise.*

*Then came also publicans to be baptized, and said unto him, Master, what shall we do? And he said unto them, Exact no more than that which is appointed you. And the soldiers likewise demanded of him, saying, And what shall we do? And he said unto them, Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages.*

John the Baptist is in the wilderness, preaching to the masses of people from all around Judea and the surrounding countries, who have come to hear the word of God preached, under the power of the Holy Ghost.

Many repent and believe and are baptized in expectation of the Christ. But they, as babes, don't know what to do, now that they are saved. What does this mean in practice? How is it applied in their lives. John says that dead trees will be hewn down and burned. Like the vipers of the Pharisees and Sadducees who do not produce any fruit, they're not bringing people to turn towards God. They aren't doing works of charity. As Jesus will later preach, they are hypocrites and worse. But those who by hearing the word of God come to faith, not wanting to be as the vipers, the fruitless, pricked in their conscience by the word, not wanting to be hewn down, they ask "What shall we do?"

And to the publicans, who were tax collectors, a group known for their overcharging, abusing their office and taking bribes, he says take no more than you're appointed to, basically to be honest in your dealings. To the soldiers, he answers in a similar manner. He says not to commit violence, or falsely accuse or to covet more than his wages. Basically, don't abuse your position of power.

Of course, all of this can be boiled down to "Love thy neighbor," which many of us overlook because it is such a basic teaching. Even unbelieving unregenerate man know the golden rule. And they knew it then, too. It was part of the law. God commanded it of them in **Leviticus 19:18**

*Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the Lord.*

But what does that look like in practice? How do we as saved Christians, at liberty in Christ, having repented of our past beliefs and acknowledged we are sinners destined to Hell but for the grace of God and are now saved, what do we do now?

And John's answer to these people, 2000 years ago, remains the answer today. In your daily life, don't defraud people. Don't steal. Don't abuse whatever authority you have, at work or at home. Don't lie. Don't behave as the vipers, hypocrites and unbelievers. Love others the way you want to be loved. The way you trust in Christ to love you.

And so, at work, do you slack? Steal time from the boss? Take advantage of your position? Lie to others? Gossip? Covet the status of wealth of others? Commit adultery? Not even that adultery of the heart Jesus warned us of?

At home, do you love your spouse as Christ loves the church? Jealously and putting their well being before your own? Honoring your parents? Not coveting your neighbors possessions?

Are you a blessing to your community? To your church family? To strangers? Are you a light that shines, magnifying God's love for you that others may come to ask you why you're full of love and hope?

**1 Peter 3:15-16**
*but sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear: having a good conscience; that, whereas they speak evil of you, as of evildoers, they may be ashamed that falsely accuse your good conversation in Christ.*

teachings.title: Love your enemies, in context
teachings.summary: After hard preaching against the crowds, Jesus told His disciples to love their enemies and judge not, meaning to show the mercy God showed us, not to ignore evil.
teachings.text:
*But woe unto you that are rich! for ye have received your consolation. Woe unto you that are full! for ye shall hunger. Woe unto you that laugh now! for ye shall mourn and weep. Woe unto you, when all men shall speak well of you! for so did their fathers to the false prophets.*

Hard preaching, fire-breathing. Jesus wasn't a dainty and soft man. His preaching went hard, the Bible says He spoke with authority. Boldness. He never hesitated to put on blast those who needed to be reproached. Fire and brimstone. Out of His mouth proceeded a two-edged sword. The word of God.

And again, He turns to His disciples and gives them a practical application for what He has given them. That these people who praised the false prophets while killing the messengers of God, and will likewise persecute those who do good in His name may be your enemies for the Gospel's sake, but that doesn't mean to hate them, but rather:

*I say unto you which hear, Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you, Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you. And unto him that smiteth thee on the one cheek offer also the other.*..

This is the part of the preaching of Christ that those who don't know or understand call "weak." They remove the context to make Jesus sound like he only taught love and peace, like a hippy. But we have the context. He's just ripped face to condemn the very masses He is serving with healing and casting out unclean spirits, for their fickleness and worldly lusts. Verily they have their reward...but blessed are those who have the Kingdom of Heaven.

He says love them, turn the other cheek, if they defraud you or spoil you (meaning to take your stuff), let them. If they persecute you, rejoice. Pity your enemies. They don't have what you got. He's saying you have it better than them and it's true. It may not seem like it in the moment. You may be hungry. You may be without, poor. You may be hated of your own family for the preaching of the Gospel.

But you're blessed.

And woe to the rich, and woe to the satisfied. Woe to those that curse the blessed, who spoil the meek, who, like their fathers, kill the prophets and reject the word of truth.

Pity them. They are perishing. They will have their reward. Eternal fire and torment without end. But we have a different fate. We have been saved by grace, a gift we didn't deserve, given by the mercy of God despite our being just as these others were. Perishing. Pulled out of the fire by His blood, and called by the Spirit that we may believe, and in faith be made heirs with Him in the Kingdom of God.

And so, *love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil. Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful.*

We were that unthankful and evil. Sure we love those who love us, and do good to them, and lend to others. But sinners do all that too. That's easy.

But we have an unearned gift, made sons of the Most High. And to whom much is given, much is expected.

*Judge not, and ye shall not be judged: condemn not, and ye shall not be condemned: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven: Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom. For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again.*

Some of the most misunderstood and misused scripture in the entire Bible. But in context we see what Jesus is saying to us. He isn't saying to simply stand for evil, not judging the actions of others, but to put in perspective their  condition with the understanding of our own.

We who are saved have been judged. We know we have fallen short. We know we needed mercy and the longsuffering of God to come to where we are. Not of ourselves. Humbled by it, we are called to be merciful as God is merciful. That's the context here.

God hates evil and gives wrath as recompense for those who hate Him. Vengeance is His.

teachings.title: The centurion's faith a model for ours
teachings.summary: The centurion's great faith came with humility and love for others, a model for us to grow our faith by caring for those sick in spirit.
teachings.text:
**Hebrews 11:1-2**
 *Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. For by it the elders obtained a good report.*

Luke chapter 7 is a study on faith. The faith of the Roman centurion. The faith of John the Baptist. The faith of those who follow him and Jesus. The faith of the Pharisees. And the faith of the woman who washed Jesus' feet. Rich in faith, and poor in faith.

Unquestioning, lacking and unsure.

The chapter opens after Jesus' sermon on the plain in Chapter 6. After he'd finished speaking, we learn of *a certain centurion's servant, who was dear unto him, was sick, and ready to die.*

*And when he heard of Jesus, he sent unto him the elders of the Jews, beseeching him that he would come and heal his servant.*

So we get the picture. A Roman centurion, a Gentile, stationed in the region, who commanded as an officer of the empire, one hundred men. A man of power and prestige, who has a servant he loves. A slave, for Roman citizens' servants were slaves. But a person he cared for dearly, who is near death. And hearing of Jesus and the miracles and signs and wonders He had done reported throughout the region, the Centurion sees hope for his friend whom he loves.

In his heart, the Centurion sees the evidence of something not seen. And his faith hangs on the substance of his hope in Jesus. And it is in this manner he uses his influence to call in a favor. He asks prominent Jews to approach Jesus and ask Him for help. Jews who he had authority over, but who the Centurion had treated well, even building for them a synagogue. And they come and testify to Jesus that this man is a good man, and worthy of His aid. And so Jesus goes with the Jews to the centurion's home. Before getting there, again the Centurion has sent proxies, this time to say "Lord, trouble not thyself: for I am not worthy that thou shouldest enter under my roof."

The man to whom others testified that he was worthy. Who we see is a loving and just man. A man of faith. Who does for others, even the lowliest of his house, a slave. This great man that others testified was worthy and just and good says, ashamed to even be in the presence of the Son of God, "I am not worthy of you, but only say the word and my servant will be healed."

Because the Centurion is familiar with power and authority. How it works, how it flows. That even by faith, power moves to achieve what his will is, that if he order men to do this or that, it is done. He can know it will be so. And so he understands by this that Jesus, who  he believes has this power, has this authority, needn't come to him to save his servant. He has faith of Jesus commands that he be healed, he will be made whole.

And Jesus, moved with compassion and wonder at his faith, turns to the Jews and others round about, and says "*I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel.*" And they return to the house to find the servant healed.

The humility and love that this man, a Gentile, showed others gave to him the understanding of who Jesus was. And the faith that such a thing would be possible led him to humbly ask for this miracle, for the good of another.

To have faith in God as strong as this, we see, comes with compassion, humility, love for others. And the Centurion's faith is a model for ours.

We come to repentance, to turn towards God in humility. With faith like a child's. Knowing that we will be healed. That faith grows in our service for others. Where we magnify the faith that saved us by doing the will of God, in service to those that are sick. Not sick of the flesh, though we are led to comfort them, but sick in the spirit. To hold others as dear to us. Not because of status or what they can do for us, but selflessly, genuinely caring for others. In that way we work out our faith that it benefiting others, may grow, and spread to them. That they may be healed as we were. By faith.

teachings.title: Pure religion: compassion for the brokenhearted
teachings.summary: Jesus raising the widow's son shows His compassion, and our mission like His in Isaiah 61 is to comfort the brokenhearted and visit the fatherless and widows.
teachings.text:
Next, we are given an example of the compassion of Christ. Almost as an aside, an interlude to the events of the chapter, we are given one of the greatest miracles of Jesus' ministry.

Jesus comes to a city with an entourage. His disciples and those who were following just to witness the wonders and signs, healing and casting out of devils. Spectators and believers alike.

And here they find a funeral procession, a bereaved mother burying her son who is being carried by pallbearers to the grave.

And the Bible says, Jesus moved with compassion for the mother approaches and touches the body and resurrects her son. In the witness of many, the Bible says Jesus raised the dead.

Many wonder at the sight, praising God. It's an unimaginable event to witness. But what strikes me every time I read it is the compassion shown of Jesus. He sees a mother heartbroken and grieving, a stranger. A woman he doesn't know. No one has sought him to intervene. No one like the centurion humbly coming before Hm.

But Jesus moved with compassion does what he can to comfort the brokenhearted. And with the power He has, He raises the boy from the dead.

This brings to mind the verse from Isaiah that Jesus read at the beginning of His ministry. What I have been calling His mission statement;

*The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord.*

And this is our mission statement too. Those who seek to follow Christ. The Bible tells us in **James 1:27**:
*Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.*

Love one another. Our neighbors. Our enemies. To entertain the stranger, because in doing so we may be entertaining the angels of God. To be, like the Centurion, someone who cares about others and uses his power that others may profit. To have compassion for the brokenhearted, and like Jesus, do what we can to comfort them.

teachings.title: Workers of Heaven, not working for Heaven
teachings.summary: Against the Pharisees' hypocrisy, we are not working for Heaven but are workers of Heaven, bought with a price to do charity and preach the gospel as in Isaiah 61.
teachings.text:
Compare Jesus assessment of the hypocritical false teachers and the hypocrisy of their religion, vs the mission statement from Isaiah 61 that Jesus began His ministry with;

*The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord.*

*Vs*

*Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone. Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel. Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess.*

We aren't supposed to be working *for* Heaven, we are supposed to be workers *of* Heaven. That the Kingdom of Heaven draw nigh them, when we do the charity and humble service to others we are called to. When we give the Gospel to the poor, and heal the broken hearted. Clothe the naked and feed those in need.

We didn't find Jesus, He found us, and set us to labor for Him, as we were bought with a price. This is the calling of discipleship that we all receive when we are saved. And yet few believers are able to commit to it. I being chief.

*Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.*

teachings.title: Sit in the lowest room; call the poor to the feast
teachings.summary: Jesus taught guests to seek the lowest seat and hosts to invite the poor who cannot repay, a pattern of the Kingdom, while the invited Jews who refused would not taste His supper.
teachings.text:
Then He gives those bidden to the supper like He was some advice in humility and how the wisdom of men differs from that of God.

Jesus says, if you're invited to a party, don't go in assuming you're asked to sit in the high places of status, instead be seated in the lowest room. Just happy to be there, and so when the lord of the supper bids you to sit in a more privileged seat, you are truly honored. If you presume, and you're asked to give up your spot to one greater than you, you will be humiliated. It's a basic teaching on how life works, and how it is in the Kingdom, that these social climbers and clout seeking Pharisees miss.

Jesus goes on to say; *when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: And thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee: for thou shalt be recompensed at the resurrection of the just.*

If you have the means to call a feast, humbly seek to serve those who cannot do anything for you. Who are week. Honor them without thought for reward in this life and be rewarded for it at the judgment. It is the counterpoint advice for hosts, paired with how guests should behave.

This pattern holds true in the Kingdom to come.

He then gives the parable of the wedding feast, where the honored guests all refuse the invitation with their excuses, the cares of the world. Those bidden refuse to come. He is speaking to the Pharisees, saying they are like them.

The feast will go on. The Lord will invite those poor and lame and of no status, that his house be filled. He will send his servants to the highways and hedges and compel the meek and lowly, bidding them to the feast. Those originally bidden, the Jews, the hypocritical religious leaders, they won't taste of this supper.

teachings.title: Correct in love, rejoice over the lost
teachings.summary: As God removes our sins as far as the east from the west, we must correct in love, forgive and forget, and rejoice when the lost return, without compromising on sin.
teachings.text:
These types drive wedges between brothers, sow discord in the assembly, and have torn down entire church families, turning off an unknown multitude from receiving the Gospel by their bad report. Placing stumbling blocks before others, reminding them of their old man constantly.

The Bible says *As far as the east is from the west, So far hath he removed our transgressions from us.* God says, *their sins and iniquities will I remember no more.*

As Jesus puts it, *Likewise, I say unto you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth.*

This must be our attitude as Christians towards others. To love with the charitable love Jesus gave us. Longsuffering. Merciful. With grace. Forgetting about the past. Not holding grudges. Being understanding of the frailties of others, knowing with humility exactly how frail we are ourselves.

This is not to say we ignore sin, or compromise what is right. There is church discipline for a reason, and it is outlined by Jesus and the epistles for our use. Right is right. If God says it's a sin, we ought have no other opinion on the matter. We teach and preach separation. Feeding the new man that the old man may fade away. Edifying one another. Steel sharpening steel.

But we correct in love. We deal with the beam in our eye so that we may help others with the mote that is in theirs. We forgive when sincere apology is made. We forget, so that there is no resentment or grudge. We avoid the leaven of hypocrisy. We celebrate the return of the lost, rejoicing in their salvation.

*It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found.*

Amen

teachings.title: Live peaceably, then call out evil
teachings.summary: By living peaceably, blamelessly and charitably and sharing what we have, we earn the respect that lets us stand for biblical truth and call out evil.
teachings.text:
*If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men. Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.*
...
*That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world; Holding forth the word of life; that I may rejoice in the day of Christ, that I have not run in vain, neither laboured in vain.*
...
*Servants, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh; not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but in singleness of heart, fearing God: and whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men; knowing that of the Lord ye shall receive the reward of the inheritance: for ye serve the Lord Christ.*

Be not afraid. Be charitable. Be merciful, longsuffering, prone to hospitality, more willing that another profit, that it glorifys God.

If you start with this basic premise and understanding, and apply it in your life, best you can, it provides you with the ability to call evil out when you see it, and have people respect and agree with you, and defend you because you you've been a blessing to them, which by your conversation, behavior, they see in you that light that shines. Taking the lesson of the parable of the unjust steward in Luke 16, as Jesus says

*And I say unto you, Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations.*

Share your wealth. Doesn't even have to be things or cash. Could be time. Compassion. Doing the things you can do for others. Love your enemies. Live blamelessly. And when things come up, stand for biblical truth.

teachings.title: Woe to him through whom offences come
teachings.summary: Mature believers must not offend babes in Christ by pride dressed as rebuke, and we must honestly own the times we caused others to stumble.
teachings.text:
In our Christian life we will be babes, and meet babes. Not everyone is at the same point as you are in your walk. Many you will meet have a head understanding of the word, and not the faith that comes from it, or they retain some of the ideas and doctrines of men that they still apply, convinced of their importance to the faith they've only just begun to have.

They are like children. Babes in Christ. And if you're more solid in your faith, have a greater understanding of the liberty found in Christ, and yet seek to impose that understanding in a way that brings that child to be offended, you're doing them harm. Woe unto you.

Honestly assess the times in your life where in judgment your rebuke and reproof was actually just pride and arrogance, and how in that sin you've brought others to sin. We can all recall times where we joined the evil of others, where we set wicked things before someone else's eyes. Where we encouraged another to join us in something we ought not do. Misery loving company. It is impossible but that offenses come, and so it is impossible but that we have been the means by which they do.

But how many of us have done this subtly, and supposedly in Christ's name? Raise your hand. If we are honest with ourselves, we all have our hands up. Few Christians can say they haven't used poor judgment that could cause another to stumble.

teachings.title: The women's looking glasses for the laver
teachings.summary: The women giving their mirrors for the laver pictures turning from vanity and self to service, being sanctified as doers of the word.
teachings.text:
*And he made the laver of brass, and the foot of it of brass, of the lookingglasses of the women assembling, which assembled at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation.*

The women gave their mirrors that they be crafted into the laver, or washing bowl for the Tabernacle. Where the priests sanctified themselves with the diverse washings of the Levitical priesthood. We are similarly called to be washed, to be sanctified as doers of the word. Turning from self, as these faithful women did by giving up the objects of their vanity, their looking glass made of polished brass, and being doers of the word, turning them in to be fitted into vessels for sanctification.

And the men, numbering 603,550, likewise turned in the shekels, their earnings for labor, that they may go to the Tabernacle in obedience to God's calling.

We are asked to turn from ourselves towards service to others. Called to follow the word of God and by doing so, sanctify ourselves towards Him. Washing as the priests washed themselves before entering into the holiest places of the Tabernacle, but in Spirit not ritual washings of the flesh.

teachings.title: Not slothful in business
teachings.summary: Freed from death we serve life by loving the brethren and working diligently for any boss as unto the Lord, laying up treasure in heaven.
teachings.text:
As we covered yesterday in the first half of chapter 12, faced with the truth of the Gospel and having repented towards God, being changed by the Spirit, sealed unto redemption, with eternity awaiting and goodwill with the Father through adoption as His sons, then we should live as His. To His purpose and glory, not frustrating the grace of God.

Not for our benefit; we don't sanctify ourselves and walk in the Spirit to save ourselves from the wages of sin, as we are justified by Christ's righteousness without works of the law, but rather being freed from that fear and the yoke we were under as servants to death, we can become servants to life.

We establish the law.

*Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.*

And so, continuing to wrest the implications of salvation, Paul writes;

*Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another*. As Jesus asked us to love our brethren in Him. We should put the profit of our brothers and sisters in Christ above our own. With humility and meekness, being ministering servants.

*Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord*.

This is not only in our service to God for His works; winning souls, edifying the brethren, ministering to the afflicted, having hospitality and a generous spirit, but literally too, at work. A Christian is an exemplary employee when they see their work is for God, and a reflection of His work in us.

**Colossians 3:22-25**
*Servants, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh; not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but in singleness of heart, fearing God; And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men; Knowing that of the Lord ye shall receive the reward of the inheritance: for ye serve the Lord Christ. But he that doeth wrong shall receive for the wrong which he hath done: and there is no respect of persons.*

The Bible doesn't say we should serve our bosses if they are saved. If they are Godly. It makes no distinction, and would apply even as slaves. We work, we don't rob our employers, because we work for God.

Note the similarity with what John the Baptist preached to the newly converted to Christ in **Luke 3**:

 *And the people asked him, saying, What shall we do then? He answereth and saith unto them, He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do likewise. Then came also publicans to be baptized, and said unto him, Master, what shall we do? And he said unto them, Exact no more than that which is appointed you. And the soldiers likewise demanded of him, saying, And what shall we do? And he said unto them, Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages.*

It's the same message.

If we love God and we understand eternity in the spirit, then this short time in the flesh is His. And if we love our neighbor, we should seek their profit above our own.

And He will repay. **Matthew 6:19-21**

*Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.*

Get the picture here, if we are humble. Meek. Knowing we are saved. Knowing the love of God and the peace in Christ, act like it.

Not in pride, dishonesty. Not taking more than we are due. Our work reflecting the Spirit of God. That we may, by example be part of that revelation from Heaven of His mercy, that His light be magnified in us, drawing others to Him.

teachings.title: The strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak
teachings.summary: Strong believers should put aside their own comfort to build up the weak, following Christ's example of meekness without compromising the truth.
teachings.text:
Romans 15 caps off the doctrines of Christ that Paul has laid out for us, the truth of God and His word, finally shared throughout the world to every nation.

Carrying over the admonishment of chapter 14, to those stronger in the faith and with better understanding of scripture to be mindful of those weaker than us, babes in Christ. Those easily led to sin by their own devices. To not judge, but support.

*We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not please ourselves.*

This is spiritual. The true religion. We put too much emphasis on our own comfort and satisfaction and not the needs of others. When Paul writes to please our neighbors, it isn't as manpleasers, not being weak and being obsequious. But being meek, and leading them for their good and edification. Building people up.

This is a hard concept for many. A healthy person can put aside their own wants and desires to make another stronger, and in doing so, shine the light of God that they may come to believe. To ask you the reason for your hope. And so whatever small things you do for them, do it with cheer and charity. Not enabling or partaking in sin, but by example as we are given by the Spirit. Just as Christ by example led us to His truth. He took the pains of our sin upon Himself, loved us, shows compassion for the afflicted, but never once backs down to say what's right. Preaching the truth in love, with all long-suffering.

teachings.title: Leave the gleanings for the poor and stranger
teachings.summary: The gleaning law is God's way of caring for the poor, and spiritually our freely given bounty may bring the lost to the truth.
teachings.text:
*And when ye reap the harvest of your land, thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field, neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy harvest. And thou shalt not glean thy vineyard, neither shalt thou gather every grape of thy vineyard; thou shalt leave them for the poor and stranger: I am the Lord your God.*

Practically, this command of the Lord is the biblical way of caring for the poor and the sojourners among the people. That they may glean, or that is, to go through a field or orchard and pick the leftover crops that hadn't been harvested by the husbandman. Allowing the corner of the land to be eaten of, not going back again and again to make sure you got all the crops that God had blessed us with.

But the spiritual application of it, in light of the New Testament and the multiple parables of Jesus regarding the harvest, shows that the blessings of the saved received of God may bring the poor and the lost some good, and perhaps lead them to the truth.

Our bounty, freely given as God so freely gave to us, shared without greed or personal consideration, without resentment. In charity and mercy. Hospitality.

We see incidents of gleaning in other scripture, including Jesus and the disciples picking corn as they went on their way on a sabbath, to the chagrin of the Pharisees. It is an important concept in both spiritual and earthly matters.

teachings.title: He that is chief, as he that doth serve
teachings.summary: Like David's mighty men and the disciples striving for position, believers may strive to do great things for the Lord, but first must seek to serve, counting the cost of suffering while pressing toward the prize.
teachings.text:
This chapter reminds me of the Apostles, constantly competing for position and favor and honor in the Kingdom of Heaven.

**Luke 9:46-48**
*Then there arose a reasoning among them, which of them should be greatest. And Jesus, perceiving the thought of their heart, took a child, and set him by him, And said unto them, Whosoever shall receive this child in my name receiveth me: and whosoever shall receive me receiveth him that sent me: for he that is least among you all, the same shall be great.*

**Luke 22:24-30**
*And there was also a strife among them, which of them should be accounted the greatest. And he said unto them, The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; and they that exercise authority upon them are called benefactors. But ye shall not be so: but he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve. For whether is greater, he that sitteth at meat, or he that serveth? is not he that sitteth at meat? but I am among you as he that serveth. Ye are they which have continued with me in my temptations. And I appoint unto you a kingdom, as my Father hath appointed unto me; That ye may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.*

**Mark 10:35-45**
*And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, come unto him, saying, Master, we would that thou shouldest do for us whatsoever we shall desire. And he said unto them, What would ye that I should do for you? They said unto him, Grant unto us that we may sit, one on thy right hand, and the other on thy left hand, in thy glory. But Jesus said unto them, Ye know not what ye ask: can ye drink of the cup that I drink of? and be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with? And they said unto him, We can. And Jesus said unto them, Ye shall indeed drink of the cup that I drink of; and with the baptism that I am baptized withal shall ye be baptized: but to sit on my right hand and on my left hand is not mine to give; but it shall be given to them for whom it is prepared. And when the ten heard it, they began to be much displeased with James and John. But Jesus called them to him, and saith unto them, Ye know that they which are accounted to rule over the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; and their great ones exercise authority upon them. But so shall it not be among you: but whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister: and whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all. For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.*

The Apostles and chief disciples of Jesus were as the mighty men of David. And we are called honor as well. We can do great things for the Lord, even strive with one another to out do each other. We can run the gauntlet of Philistines to bring water for our Lord, but first we should seek to serve. First we should seek to be a good judge for the children, the fatherless, the widows. A servant to our brethren.

And we should be cautious in what we strive for, as the sons of Thunder, James and John sought. The baptism of pain and persecution may be the price for glory. The cup of tribulation and suffering for His name. But even so, we should reach for the prize set before us;

**1 Corinthians 9:24-27**
*Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain. And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible. I therefore so run, not as uncertainly; so fight I, not as one that beateth the air: but I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.*

**Philippians 3:13-14**
*Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.*

teachings.title: Heap coals of fire on his head
teachings.summary: Unlike Jonah, believers must show mercy to enemies, including giving them the bread of life and water of the gospel, remembering the mercy God showed them.
teachings.text:
**Matthew 5:44-45**
*But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you; That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.*

**Romans 9:15-16**
*For he saith to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion. So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.*

**Proverbs 25:21-23**
*If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink: For thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the Lord shall reward thee. The north wind driveth away rain: so doth an angry countenance a backbiting tongue.*

Perhaps the hardest thing in the Christian life, showing mercy to those who hate us and whom we hate. But if God chooses us to be a blessing to another, it isn't on us to question why. We shouldn't be as Jonah.

And if they are hardened against us, that's on them. Our mercy will be as hot coals upon their head.

**Romans 12:20**
*Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head.*

Note the spiritual application of this. Your enemy hungers and thirsts. For what? Food and water? Or truth and the repentance unto faith in Christ?

Will the coals of fire make them angrier and dug in against you? Or remind them of the Hell that awaits them?

Will you withhold that bread that came down from Heaven? The waters of life that you've drank?

Are there many who don't know their right hand from left?

Only God knows.

Remember the mercy God showed you, and let that be what guides your spirit. Don't be as Jonah, and let your anger consume you.

teachings.title: Usury and forgiving our debtors
teachings.summary: God's people should not take usury or unjust gain from the poor but give cheerfully and forgive debts, as God has forgiven us.
teachings.text:
This even extended to making a profit on food sold to the poor;

**Leviticus 25:35-37**
*And if thy brother be waxen poor, and fallen in decay with thee; then thou shalt relieve him: yea, though he be a stranger, or a sojourner; that he may live with thee. Take thou no usury of him, or increase: but fear thy God; that thy brother may live with thee. Thou shalt not give him thy money upon usury, nor lend him thy victuals for increase.*

Land owners were expected to allow gleaning of their fields, that after a harvest, the poor should go through the fields and bring in anything left behind by the laborers.

Alms and feasts of charity are expected of the Lord's people. Forgiveness of debts. A cheerful giver, providing for those in need is praised.

**Proverbs 11:25-27**
*The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself. He that withholdeth corn, the people shall curse him: but blessing shall be upon the head of him that selleth it.*

As **Proverbs 28:8** promises;

*He that by usury and unjust gain increaseth his substance, he shall gather it for him that will pity the poor*.

The gain you may make is temporary. The Lord will make certain your wealth is distributed to the righteous, in the end.

Because God is so just to forgive us, we should love one another enough to be like Him.

**Luke 7:41-42**
*There was a certain creditor which had two debtors: the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty. And when they had nothing to pay, he frankly forgave them both. Tell me therefore, which of them will love him most?*

So, we should not seek unjust gain, and further, we should relieve those in our debt, as God has forgiven us.

**Matthew 6:9-13**
*After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.*

teachings.title: Defend the widow and the fatherless
teachings.summary: God's call to defend and provide for the widow, the fatherless and the needy is the outward practice He expects of believers, and He desires this mercy rather than the vain rituals and sacrifices of works-based religion.
teachings.text:
The reoccurring theme of the Lord defending the widow, the fatherless and the poor, and our role in carrying out righteous judgment for them, is probably the most talked about doctrine outside of Who God is, and the doctrines of salvation in Christ.

More than anything else, we are to clothe and feed the truly needy, to make sure people don't take advantage of those who have no one to defend them. No husband, no father. To do unto the least of these, and in doing so, doing it for Jesus.

**James 1:27**
*Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.*

This is the ultimate expression of our faith. The outward practice God expects. Self-sacrifice for others, not the selfish sacrifice of the works-based religions of the world.

**Hosea 6:6**
*For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings*

All the penance and "Eucharist" sacrifices, and all the other rites and rituals men do to get the Lord to be pleased with them are vain. God wants us to exercise mercy and judgment.

**Proverbs 21:3**
*To do justice and judgment is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice.*

Jesus, reading Isaiah, gives us the mission statement for Christians;

Luke 4:18–19
*The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord.*

Amen

teachings.title: Delight in the saints, not Lordship salvation
teachings.summary: Calling Jesus Lord is a saved believer's statement of fact, not the false gospel of Lordship salvation; our good works add nothing to God but are poured out in love and service to the saints.
teachings.text:
**Psalm 16** presents another sacred hymn celebrating the Lord's salvation, the eternal security of the believer, and the promise of the risen Christ.

The preservation of the saints is the hope of all who place their trust in God. Our very being cries out to Him for salvation, recognizing He is Lord.

Note here that this isn't "Lordship salvation," a false gospel that says you must "make Jesus the Lord of your life" to be saved. It is saved believers, already trusting Him to save us, recognizing that He IS the Lord, as a statement of fact.

David writes, *Thou art my Lord: my goodness extendeth not to thee; But to the saints that are in the earth, and to the excellent, in whom is all my delight.* The good that we do isn't for Him, it adds nothing to the holy and perfect God.

The idea that Jesus needs us to make Him Lord, that by our "turning from sin," we justify ourselves before God, is hubris. It's a false gospel.

The good we do comes from Him, and is poured out to the brothers and sisters, the saints. We benefit others, and they glorify God. We obey His judgements, to one another's profit.

**Matthew 5:16**
*Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.*

We submit ourselves to the righteousness of God. We do not seek to establish our own righteousness, but to magnify His.

**Romans 10:3–4**
*For they being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth.*

David's burden is for the saints in the earth, his delight is to the excellent of God. Just as we are commanded to.

**John 13:34–35**
*A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.*

While we should seek to live peaceably with all men, we should especially look with love upon our fellow believers.

**Galatians 6:9–10**
*And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not. As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.*

This is the message that we have heard from the beginning. It is our job as Christians. It is how we are to know one another. Not keeping to ourselves or seeking out own profit. Certainly not by hating our brothers.

1 John 3:10–11
*In this the children of God are manifest, and the children of the devil: whosoever doeth not righteousness is not of God, neither he that loveth not his brother. For this is the message that ye heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.*

This is the mind of Christ, to be servants, one to another. To delight in others.

The ultimate expression of humility isn't thinking less of yourself, but not thinking of yourself at all. And the humbleness of submission to God's righteousness should naturally turn to our service for others. Not to add to God's goodness our filthy rags, but to glorify His goodness in us.

teachings.title: The desires of thine heart
teachings.summary: When we trust the Lord and do good, our heart's desires become His, turning from our own lusts to pure religion and good works done for others so they glorify God.
teachings.text:
God promises those that trust in Him and do good will be given the desires of our hearts.

**Jeremiah 17:9–10**
*The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings.*

When we are right with God, and do according to His ways, our heart's desires are His. They are upright and good, because our will becomes His when in all our ways we acknowledge Him, and allow the Lord to direct our paths.

He tries the reins, and sees our good works and rewards us openly. We consider the poor and broken-hearted. We take up the cause of the fatherless and widows. We spread the good news of eternal life in Christ Jesus. We live lives separated unto the gospel, and consider the profit of others above our own. Our desires become for the good of others.

*Lord help me to live from day to day*
*In such a self-forgetful way,*
*That even when I kneel to pray*
*My prayer shall be for others*.

This hymn encapsulates the concept.

**James 1:27**
*Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.*

When we consider others, when we love our neighbors and even our enemies, when we practice pure religion, the outward works of our faith, it should be for others.

And our keeping ourselves from the filth of the world is part of that, that God will see our good works, and give us our desires, and make all things come to pass.

*He shall bring forth thy righteousness as the light, and thy judgment as the noonday.*

We are the light of the world. Our purpose is to magnify the light within us that others, yes others, see it and glorify God.

**Matthew 5:16**
*Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.*

By trusting the Lord and doing good, we preserve our nation, we get to dwell in the land, we are fed, and we see our hearts turn from desiring our own wicked lusts, to seeking good for others.

teachings.title: Blessed is he that considereth the poor
teachings.summary: God blesses those who help the poor out of unfeigned charity rather than to be seen, because the heart behind the giving is what He rewards.
teachings.text:
**Psalm 41** is brief and to the point. David opens with the doctrine of the Lord's promise to preserve and give long life on the earth to those of His people who consider the poor. Who show mercy to the widows and take up the cause of the fatherless.

Just as the commandment to honor your parents comes with a promise, that it be well with you and lengthen your days, this practice of pure religion, to consider the poor, comes with a similar blessing.

Basic stuff, which we are told over and over again in scripture, because it often is the hardest thing for man to do; love the unlovable the way God loves us.

**Luke 14:13–14**
*But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: And thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee: for thou shalt be recompensed at the resurrection of the just*.

The act of giving alms or feeding the poor is not itself what gives us blessings. Many may be generous in their actions, to be seen of men or to make themselves self-righteous.

Helping people who cannot help you back out of love, is love unfeigned. It is the charity Paul calls us to. The selfless, sacrificial love for God and others, in your heart. More so than the actual alms or donation of goods. The spirit behind it is everything.

**1 Corinthians 13:3**
*And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.*

So we see that the love behind the care given to the poor, is rewarded with strengthening us in our sickness, delivering us from our enemies, God showing to us the mercy we showed those who could never repay us for the kindness.

Those that do it for their own reasons, have their reward. But the heart behind it is what God wants from us.

**Matthew 25:40**
*And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me*.

**Proverbs 19:17**
*He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the Lord; and that which he hath given will he pay him again.*

God loves a cheerful giver, one who isn't seeking anything for himself.

**Proverbs 22:9**
*He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed; for he giveth of his bread to the poor.*

But those that oppress the poor, God hates.

**Proverbs 14:31**
*He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker: but he that honoureth him hath mercy on the needy*

teachings.title: Unto whomsoever much is given
teachings.summary: The nearer a believer draws to God the more blessings He gives, and the more is required of him, yet His yoke is light.
teachings.text:
I think, for me at least, this is one of the hardest things about living a Godly Christian life. We talk about how the more spiritual you become the closer you draw yourself to God the closer He draws to you, and the greater the gifts He bestows on you in reward for your faith. We received salvation, then we received blessings upon blessings, we received knowledge and wisdom, answers to prayer. But *unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required.*

The stronger you grow in your faith the larger the burden you're expected to tow. But even then, His yoke is light in comparison to the glory we are given in grace.

teachings.title: Lovest thou me? Feed my sheep
teachings.summary: Like Peter going back to fishing, saved believers drift into the world, but Christ restores them to feed His sheep and win souls, and each should follow Him without comparing himself to others.
teachings.text:
The final chapter in the Gospel of John is a kind of postscript to John's account of his time with Jesus during His earthly ministry and after His resurrection, a personal recounting of one of the appearances of the risen Christ, and a redemption arc for the apostle Peter.

Now, during this time, after having been shown their faith wasn't in vain, that Jesus is the Christ and the Son of God, but prior to His final ascension on Pentecost, it seems that some of the disciples, Simon Peter chief among them, grew restless absent their Lord. Jesus appeared unto them but wasn't the ever present fixture leading them He had been for the past 3 years. Yes they were saved, yes they knew they had salvation, and yes they knew God's word was true, and yet when left to their own devices, Peter and the others returned to their old ways. Gone a fishing.

This is something many if not most newer Christians experience, or even young Christians brought up in the faith. The rush of joy and the zeal for our Lord gives way to our habits and old life, or, without direction fades to mundane tasks of this world instead of living for the God who bought them.

As David, a man after God's own heart wrote: *Restore unto me the joy of Thy salvation; and uphold me with Thy free spirit.* It happens to the best of us. That level of zeal is difficult to maintain at times.

Peter, one of the greatest Christians, who did so much for the Lord experienced this, and his leadership role lead him to take others along with him, back to the everyday life they'd left behind following Jesus. Not backslidden in sin necessarily, but back to the grind of the world. Carnal but not sinful. More aimless than lost. And here Jesus intervenes.

After an unsuccessful night of fishing, Jesus appears on the shore and in a familiar manner to earlier stories in the Gospels, He directs them to cast their empty nets another way, and they are amazed at the fill of the catch.

I think this is both real and a picture of the ministry to come in the great commission and the disciples being "fishers of men." That where there's sparsity of "fish" among the Jews, Jesus is showing them that casting a wider net out in a different direction, to the Gentiles, that the nets will be overflowing and yet not burst. As many fish as they can haul in.

Jesus dines with Peter, John, Thomas and the others, feeding them bread and fish He provides, over the fire He built. A picture of things.

The risen Christ is a bodily resurrection, Jesus eats. He's not a ghost or spirit, but risen in the flesh.

After they eat, Jesus tempts Peter three times with the question "*Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?"* And Peter, three times, swears that he does, and that Jesus knows that he does. Just as Peter had denied Jesus thrice before the cock crowed just weeks earlier, Jesus has given him a chance to redeem himself, and direction for his life if he truly loved Jesus. "Feed my sheep."

This is the direction given to all saved believers, to be part of that royal priesthood. To be His disciples. To share the Gospel and win the souls of those lost sheep. To be fishers of men. It's a personal and touching form of the great commission.

Jesus indicates to Peter where his discipleship shall lead, and John as narrator explains to the reader that it's to a martyrs death that glorified God if Peter follows Him. If he feeds His sheep.

With that understanding, Jesus says "Follow me," and Peter does, with John coming along.

Here we see another instance of Peters personality, why Jesus named him a stone. Peter, processing the death he should die for his following Jesus and feeding His sheep turns and points to John and says basically, "what about him?" It's classic Simon Peter.

Jesus' reply, "*If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee? follow thou me."* is a gentle rebuke and reminder that we aren't to worry so much about how other saved Christians walk their Christian life, but rather concentrate on our own. If one does nothing, that's not excuse for ourselves.

teachings.title: Put off the old man, put on the new
teachings.summary: Grown in the unity of the faith, believers walk not as the reprobate who are past feeling but as new men convicted by the Spirit, putting away lying, wrath and corrupt communication.
teachings.text:
And so with that unity of faith, in the knowledge of the Son of God, *That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive; But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ.*

And so we should walk in that truth, live the love we have received. Not as others in the world who are captive by the *vanity of their mind*. The foolish doctrines of man. The ignorance that comes from *the blindness of their heart*. Not walking as the reprobate does, *being past feeling,* given over to *lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness.*

In grace, through Jesus, we have a new man, created by the Spirit, and that Spirit convicts us in our sin, where the reprobate is past feeling, we are made all the more sensitive to God's will, a new man made with righteousness.

And so Paul encourages we put off lying, wrath, stealing, envy, corrupt communication, that is speech that tears down rather than edifying others. Speech that puts blame on us and hinders others faith, we shouldn't engage in.

So, with our conscience quickened, *grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption. Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.*

teachings.title: Set your affection on things above
teachings.summary: Saved believers mortify the lusts of the flesh, put on the new man, and show it in honest dealing, godly homes and diligent work done for the Lord.
teachings.text:
Paul's focus shifts to now-familiar themes. If we be saved, children of light, then seek the things of Heaven. The word of God. The glory of Jesus. The resurrection to come and being raptured, caught up, into the clouds with Him in glory.

For this cause, we should mortify our members against sin of the flesh, even as Jesus preached (later in today's Matthew study), "if an eye offend thee, pluck it out." We who are heirs keep our bodies in submission and our thoughts to what's pure, good and holy.

Lusts of the flesh, lust, which is the longing for what's not yours, worshiping in the Idolatry of covetousness. As it is written, in **James 4**:

*From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members? Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have, and cannot obtain: ye fight and war, yet ye have not, because ye ask not. Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts.*

These sins are the reason for God's wrath upon the children of disobedience to the Gospel, but we are children of the light, the shining city in the hill. The light we have inside is a reflection and magnifying of the love God shines on us, so don't hide it, but hold it high for all to see that they might be partakers with us. Putting off anger, wrath,Malice, blasphemy, filthy conversation, the behavior of the unsaved that acts as a bushel to hide our light and turn some away from the truth within us.

We put on the new man, have honest dealings with one another ("Let your yea be yea, and your nay, nay" - also Matt 5), doing everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, in thanks to God the Father by Christ's name.

And if we are in the new man, and we have put away the lusts of the flesh, if we mortify our members, having honest dealings with one another, edifying with songs of praise and teaching the doctrines of God in psalms, our light shining as a guide to the truth for others to follow, then what does this look like?

Wives submitting to their husbands, husbands loving their wives, children honoring their parents, fathers judging their children righteously,not in wrath, not frustrating them, but as God the Father has loved you.

And, at work? Heartily and without malice or anger, do what you're asked, because we work for God, already rewarded with the kingdom of which we are heirs. Diligently and honestly setting out to complete what is required of you, with joy and a meek spirit and the confidence of your salvation.

Those who do wrong will have their reward, just as you will for your faithful service. God is not a respecter of persons, and master or boss or elected leader, all alike will face His wrath for their transgressions. That's not on us to determine. It is on us to account for ourselves in all that we do, because we do it in Jesus' name.

Many bristle at this. Be the best husband, wife, child, employee, neighbor, regardless of whatever else. Being blameless. Not dimming the reflection of the light that you walk in. *If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.*

teachings.title: Peter slept: watch and pray lest ye deny Him
teachings.summary: Peter denied Christ after failing to watch and pray, and believers who fall asleep spiritually likewise deny Him, so we must stay vigilant in prayer; the Lord's supper is a symbol, not literal blood.
teachings.text:
Here we have Mark's version of events leading to the crucifixion of Jesus. Like most of Mark, it is condensed but packed with narrative and meaning.

Like some of Mark's Gospel, details change slightly from the other three, though all of it is there. The difference in timing and point of view, but the testimony the same. Unlike those who came to bear false witness against Christ before the high priests.

We see the familiar anointing by the woman with the precious oils. Hear of Judas' decision to betray Him because of it. See the last supper feast, Jesus breaking the bread and blessing the wine, saying He won't drink the new wine, fresh juice of the vine, again until He drinks it in the Kingdom of God. And while Jesus says the bread represents His body, broken on the cross, and the wine, the blood to be shed of the new testament, He clearly doesn't believe it is literally His blood, or else why say that?

Christianity is not a cannibal cult.

Jesus goes to pray, exceedingly sorrowful at His fate, but resigned to it. Peter and the others sleep when they should be on watch. Peter swears he would die with Jesus, but He tells Peter of his future denials, knowing all things that must happen.
Judas betrayal with a kiss. The ear of one of the guards cut off. The disciples scatter.

He is arrested. A detail found only in Mark, a boy wrapped in a linen blanket appears and the guards go to grab him, but he runs off naked. It is an odd account but most believe that a young Mark is that boy, his mother's house being in Jerusalem (**Acts 12:12**).

Next we see the false accusations, but Jesus condemned by the truth that He is the Christ. I believe this is important, that they did not turn Jesus over to be crucified for false claims and lies, but they murdered the Son of God for the truth that He was Christ.

In the garden, 3 times Peter swears he will stay with Jesus unto death. Jesus tells him to watch and pray that he be not tempted. Yet three times Peter is found sleeping. Peter denies Jesus 3 times when called out, breaking that vow.

Had he stayed awake, watching, praying, perhaps Peter then would have had the courage to not deny Christ and honor his vows. In the previous chapter, Jesus warns us the same as Peter, to keep watch for Him. To be vigilant and sober and ready for persecution that will inevitably come for those who standfast in His name as we await Jesus return. To pray for the strength to suffer without fear.

And most of us, like Peter, read that admonition in Mark 13, and vow to God in ourselves that we will surely be vigilant, and never back down or deny Him, even unto death. Just as Peter does in the garden.

And just like Peter, many Christians, if not all, have periods in their lives where we fall asleep, spiritually. Where we are accused by the unsaved in Jesus' name, and deny Him. Where our vows of vigilance and devotion are forgotten and abandoned. And when we are reminded of Jesus's words, we fall to our knees weeping, like Peter, understanding how unworthy we are of Christ.

So, let us learn the lesson of Peter, to stay awake and in prayer that we may not fail when tempted, that we remain vigilant for His return. That we won't deny Him when troubles come because we love Him that the world hates.

teachings.title: We slip, but walk in the word daily
teachings.summary: Believers make vows and backslide, but walking daily in the word and prayer builds faith so we are not easily tempted and are transformed by the renewing of the mind.
teachings.text:
This dichotomy of the believer, knowing the sacrifice and given the gift of eternal life anyway through God's unearned grace, through faith in Jesus, often make commitments to turn from sin. To sacrifice our comfort, wealth and possessions, even relationships, to show our love for Jesus. Vows made, despite the Bible's warnings. Good intentions, often gone astray.

We slip. We backslide. We feed the old man, neglecting the new. We have the Spirit inside of us, God's word before us and Jesus by our side, ready to carry us. And yet, for all this advantage, we turn back towards the world.

But, the Bible says if we walk in the word daily. In prayer and supplication. Growing faith on top of faith. Building on the foundation laid by Jesus, we won't be as easily tempted. We won't fail when tested. And we will not fall into sin to be accused of, and rightly punished for, but rather suffer patiently for Jesus'name, and in doing so, be pleasing to God.

So we are called to pick up our cross daily. To *be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.*

teachings.title: Enoch walked with God
teachings.summary: Enoch, translated by faith and prophet of Christ's coming, is the example of walking separated and pleasing God, and the patriarchs picture the steps of coming to Christ.
teachings.text:
