He says he was alive once without the law, we all have been. Innocent children who don't know there is a right from wrong, do no sin. But when the knowledge of the law comes, and they in the flesh choose sin, the spirit dies to the law.

Had Adam and Eve not had the commandment in the garden, they wouldn't have sinned in eating the apple. Had the laws of God not come onto Noah and then Moses, showing us His light, we wouldn't know our flesh of the old man leads us to darkness. The law itself is holy and true. And being saved, our spirit is willing but our flesh is weak.

The old man still reigns in our members. Our flesh.

Sin takes advantage of the law to show we lust in the flesh. Not that the law is evil, but we are.

And like Paul, we do what we would not. We don't do what we should, despite wanting to. Without the newness of spirit we can't.

*For I know that in me (that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing: for to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not.*

As Jesus admonished the Apostles who were to keep watch as He prayed at Gethsemane, who fell asleep multiple times;

**Matthew 26:41**
*Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.*

teachings.title: We sin every day
teachings.theme: The old man and the new
teachings.summary: Sinless perfection is impossible in the flesh, but walking in the Spirit through prayer, scripture, church and soul winning makes the flesh easier to mortify.
teachings.text:
It is important to know as a Christian, we are not perfect and sinless perfection isn't possible in our flesh.

We all are sinners. We all deserve death and Hell but in Christ we are given His righteousness that we may be given justification before God.

We sin, every day. But unlike the unsaved (which we were and should never forget the mercy we were shown, that we not think too highly of ourselves before the unsaved), we have the Spirit within us, and our own spiritual new man cries out to do good.

But to the flesh, we are called to sin.

What do we do? The Bible says if we walk in the spirit, feeding that new man, praying, studying scripture, going to church to be edified with the congregation, practicing true religion which is care for the poor, widows, fatherless, and most importantly sharing the Gospel with others that they may be comforted as we are by the promise, that the flesh becomes easier to mortify. To subdue.

teachings.title: The fruits of the Spirit are not automatic
teachings.theme: The old man and the new
teachings.summary: Even Paul struggled with sin, so good works and victory over sin are a daily choice to walk in the Spirit, and when we fall we confess and are forgiven.
teachings.text:
And just one more point that I've touched on here but needs to seriously be stressed; the fruits of the Spirit don't come automatically.. Just because we are saved doesn't mean that we will do good. Just as it doesn't mean we will stop sinning.

Paul, who many consider the greatest Christian of all time for his understanding of God's word, writes of himself here in Romans chapter 7;

*But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members.*

Writing in **1 Timothy 1:15**
*This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.*

Paul and the other authors of the epistles write to be edifying to the brethren, that they *should* do good, that they *should not* do evil. That we *should* walk in the spirit that we do not fulfill the lusts of the flesh.

This is a choice. As Jesus says;

**Luke 9:23**
*And he said to them all, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.*

It's a daily choice. It is on us to reject the temptations of the flesh by walking in the spirit.

But it is not automatic. Even Paul struggled with sin.

So many people beat themselves up for failing to stop sin in their life. For falling short. But what does the Bible tells us? That all fall short.

**1 John 1:9**
*If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness*.

And so we are instructed; *Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh.*

And when we stumble, confess to God who has adopted us as sons, and He will forgive us and help us with our infirmities.

Don't allow the men of this world to judge your walk, and in doing so place stumbling blocks and snares for you. Those hypocrites have their reward. Instead, every day make a commitment to walk in the spirit, do for others, what you can. And give glory to God for His righteousness and mercy, in Christ Jesus. The rest will sort itself out.

teachings.title: Receive the weak in faith, not to doubtful disputations
teachings.summary: Romans 14 teaches believers not to judge or argue with brethren over matters scripture leaves open, but to bear with weaker consciences and not put stumbling blocks before them.
teachings.text:
Romans chapter 14 is Paul giving particular application to these things regarding the consequences of our faith, turning it inwardly onto brothers in Christ; our role in edifying one another rather than debating and striving in doubtful disputations about things not clearly taught in scripture.

Something we see ourselves in any church or fellowship with other churches or individual Christians.

The Bible says we are to be a *whole body fitly joined together*, repeatedly stating we should be of one mind regarding the Gospel and the ministry of it. That if there are disputes between us, or trespasses against us, that we work it out within the congregation. Even unto church discipline. But in all things we are to strive together for the Gospel, and because of this, and loving one another, we shouldn't judge one another over things the Bible isn't firm on.

Understand that the Bible is the final authority on all matters of faith and practice. All scripture is given by God that we may be throughly furnished to all good works. Perfect. Complete. Especially with the catch-all, love each other as you love yourself. Putting others needs before your own. And the profit of others before yours. As much as possible live peaceably with all men.

And so, chapter 14 begins with a hypothetical situation to illustrate the point Paul is building to.

*Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.*

This caveat  is important to understand what he is proposing; A person weak in the faith may hold themselves to a higher standard than the Bible calls for, that we being more stable in the faith may see as silly.

Right up front Paul is warning not to use the occasion to argue with them. Especially of they are so weak of faith, or babes, that either may dig in their heels at rebuke, and add to the Gospel their opinions. Doubtful disputations, arguments about unimportant things that ultimately rest on "if you disagree you aren't saved."

Get the picture here. We can assume these are both saved Christians who simply disagree on a matter of separation and sanctification that aren't spelled out, explicitly or implicitly in scripture. Paul uses eating of meat vs vegetarians, but He also applies it to celebration of holidays, even the first day of the week as sacred.

Other than the strong admonishment against eating meat sacrificed to idols in 1 Corinthians for example, even if you don't think the idol is anything but wood or molten metal, is clear. And the giving to us that all food is clean and good to eat, that is blessed in Christ by our thanksgiving, there is nothing that says we have to eat meat. Just as there's nothing against abstaining.

But one weak in the faith and consumed by guilt at eating an animal, or who sees holidays as unnecessary or even wrong in their conscience, we should be patient with. We shouldn't push them to do what's wrong in their mind, to stumble. Even if you think they're fools.

To love them, we shouldn't place stumbling blocks but rather edify them. Our job isn't to judge one another who believe and are not in open sin regarding clear teachings, over petty matters.

An example may be something like *The woman shall not wear that which pertaineth unto a man*, and applying it to all things, even specifically women's attire that has a shared element to what the male version is. Tee-shirts. Sweatshirts. Hoodies. Taking it beyond not crossdressing and wearing modest apparel as scripture teaches, but extending it to a higher level.

Just because they have a higher standard than the Bible calls for doesn't mean you should mock it or ridicule it, and by God if it is in your church and it is their standards and it isn't being placed as a work of righteousness, than not only remain quiet about it, but hold to it. Better to dress in the manner that is greater than the Bible calls for than to sow discord among the brethren and bring others to sin.

teachings.title: Do not judge another man's servant
teachings.summary: In matters of liberty such as holidays, both the stronger and the weaker believer must stop judging each other, since each gives account to God.
teachings.text:
And by the same token, those weaker in the faith should learn not to judge another's walk, if it is keeping with the spirit of the law, but maybe not to your liking.

We are to build each other up.

Stand fast for what's true, in love. If the Bible says it and they are against it. Correct them.

If the Bible gives us liberty to determine for ourselves what's right (again outside clear teachings) then don't worry about others who don't see it yet.

If you celebrate Christmas or Thanksgiving, and do it to Christ, giving thanks to God, and someone else doesn't, it shouldn't bother you. Or vice versa.

We will give account to God. Don't judge His servants by your own terms. If some brothers see it as unclean and you don't, both being fully persuaded, let the matter settle, but the onus is on both to not give the other occasion to stumble at their own conscience.

teachings.title: Encourage, do not scorn, those weaker in the faith
teachings.summary: Believers who take sanctification seriously should edify rather than scorn those who are weaker or fearful, speaking the truth in love and saving rebuke for clear doctrine.
teachings.text:
This can be very hard for many. Especially those who, despite being saved and understanding their righteousness is as filthy rags, take their sanctification in all things very seriously. They see some, in their mind, abuse the liberty we have been given in Christ. Those who do not strive as they strive. Who don't go to church as much as they do. Who don't read the Bible sufficiently enough for them. Who go soul winning sporadically, if at all when you're out there grinding.

Those people need your encouragement. Not your scorn, least we think better of ourselves than we ought. Becoming hypocrites. Edify them and show them the blessings of the work that they may emulate you.

People who take matters of this life and this world too seriously, who worry about money. Who worry about politics. Who, being weak in the faith feel like we have to be active in supporting candidates to keep "evil from gaining" or something. Who are prepping a bunker and are terrified of persecution, stocking up on ammo and freeze dried food. These to me are people weak in the faith, and I try not to judge. I have been there myself.

And while it is important to be ready for things that may happen, and aware of what's going on, to be afraid and give in to the troubles of the world is wrong. But many weak in the faith do it and believe they are serving God when they do. We should receive them, but not to doubtful disputations. Not in strife. I am using examples of how to apply this, and if they aren't perfect don't judge me.

*But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things...*

Try saying something like "I'm not judging you, but I can show you from the Bible what the word says." But don't argue. Save admonishment for actual clear doctrines, not your opinions, and not to lord over someone who isn't as far along in their Christian walk as you. (Or who. Being stronger in the faith, acting in that faith but to you, seems wrong)

teachings.title: Jeremiah 10 is not about Christmas trees
teachings.summary: Jeremiah 10 condemns carved idols, not decorative trees, so believers may celebrate Christ's birth in good conscience and others should not judge them.
teachings.text:
**Colossians 2:16-23**
*Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ. Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind, and not holding the Head, from which all the body by joints and bands having nourishment ministered, and knit together, increaseth with the increase of God. Wherefore if ye be dead with Christ from the rudiments of the world, why, as though living in the world, are ye subject to ordinances, (touch not; taste not; handle not; which all are to perish with the using;) after the commandments and doctrines of men? Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.*

There are many false teachers, Reddit theologians and sincere but misled believers, who have taken **Jeremiah 10** out of context, to make the claim that this chapter isn't about graven images, carved, fashioned and decked with plated gold and silver, idols that are being worshipped and feared as if they have power, and saying that it is explicitly about the tradition of the Christmas tree.

That it is, preaching against decorating your house with a plant while celebrating the birth of Christ Jesus. That the practice of having house plants and decorative trees is itself paganism. But what does God instruct?

**Isaiah 60:13**
*The glory of Lebanon shall come unto thee, the fir tree, the pine tree, and the box together, to beautify the place of my sanctuary; and I will make the place of my feet glorious.*

The Bible doesn't teach against use of plants as decoration. It shows us God uses evergreen trees to beautify His temple.

No one bows and serves a decorative house plant, they beautify their homes with them. No one worships a pine tree except pagan "druid" LARPers.

Even the most secular reprobate consumerist, who strips Christ from Christmas and makes it entirely about snowmen and reindeer and coveting things, doesn't look at the plastic tree covered in lights and tinsel in the corner of their living room and thinks, "I shall worship this." They don't even "venerate" it.

But that hasn't stopped some from judging believers in respect to holy days, and teaching doctrine of men for commandments.

There are plenty of reasons to not want to participate in traditional Christmas trappings, especially as they have become in the modern, consumerist world of greed. The lie of Santa, the works-based system that you have to be good, "repent of your sins or you don't get a present!" The profane and the blasphemous way our Jewish-subverted culture has secularized it all.

But most believing Christians see the season as simply a feast celebrating the miracle of the birth of our Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ.

Most take the season to reflect on scripture, give thanksgiving to God the Father for His Son, to sing Psalms and hymns praising Him. And decorating their homes, eating special meals with family. And giving gifts in the spirit of grace, just as God has given to each of us.

If you don't want to worship Jesus this way, and if you are convinced of yourself that it is a sin, then you should not do it.

And regardless of your conviction, **Romans 14** should apply;

*1 Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.*

*2 For one believeth that he may eat all things: another, who is weak, eateth herbs.*

*3 Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth: for God hath received him.*

*4 Who art thou that judgest another man's servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth. Yea, he shall be holden up: for God is able to make him stand.*

*5 One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.*

teachings.title: Doers of the word, and not hearers only
teachings.summary: James calls saved believers to ask God for wisdom in faith and to grow complete by doing the word, visiting the fatherless and widows and not being respecters of persons, noting that saved in James often means delivered from trials, not justified.
teachings.text:
James teaches the lesson that in faith, we may ask God for knowledge and understanding. That all wisdom comes from God is established in **Proverbs 2:6**

*For the LORD giveth wisdom: out of his mouth cometh knowledge and understanding.*

He cautions that we ask in faith, unwavering. Not half in, half out as some Christians are, believing the truth of the Gospel, but hedging their bets in the world. That a double minded man is unstable in all his ways. To be perfect and gain understanding we must commit to building up, faith on faith, while remaining humble, to not thinking you deserve God to just hand it to you.

That lesson in humility carries on, that the poor should rejoice in gratitude for their salvation in God's grace, while the rich, in understanding that they are but dust, and with the same meekness and humility.

He says again that the temptations and tests of this life are a blessing, that we are rewarded with the crown of life for our efforts. As Paul says in **Romans 4**, when we do His work, it is reckoned of debt, and we are paid for it by God, as His laborers. We rejoice in the free gift given by Him in grace, but receive rewards for our patience in temptation.

He warns against blaming God for our affliction, even as God blesses, He tempts no man with evil.

James tells us that it is our lusts that lead to sin, and sin to death and tribulations come from this cycle. But the gifts that come from God are blessings, given in His grace.

That we have the word of Truth, that is Christ Jesus, was beget of God's own will, that we may be His first fruits of the harvest. Amen

And so, we should avoid wrath and be patient. Avoid temptation of lust for the things of this world, and receive the word, "*engrafted*" in our hearts, *which is able to save your souls.* This is not just the Gospel and spiritual righteousness, but living in the word, obeying His law written in our hearts, saves us in the physical sense from the temptations and trials James is warning against.

Salvation, or being saved, is not always referring to the righteousness imputed on us by Jesus' blood, through faith. It often means being saved in a literal sense, as we'd use it today.

We are admonished *to be doers of the word, and not hearers only*. Many Christians go to church, sit through Bible study, and simply never grow because they are hearers only. They think they are complete Christians for their idle listening, while doing no soul winning, no charity, having no grace for others, being respecters of persons, esteeming those with power, wealth, credentials, etc, over the poor, the ignorant, those of low estate. This theme of not being a respecter of persons is another that James is hammering home in this epistle.

We are blessed in our deeds, being doers of the word.

We are called to not just be loudmouth Holy Rollers, judging everyone without grace, and puffing ourselves up for attending church, listening to preaching, and the other trappings of religion, without doing that which we are called to do. To visit the fatherless and the widow in their affliction and to keep ourselves unspotted from the world. To be a perfect, a more complete Christian, we should do the good works we are made for, as those justified by faith.

teachings.title: Built on the rock: doers of His sayings
teachings.summary: Those who hear Jesus' sayings and do them build on a rock and will not be moved, while hearers only build on sand.
teachings.text:
Finally, Jesus challenges His disciples, and by extension those of us who call ourselves His followers. He asks pointedly:

*And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?*

He is giving us the truth. The word of God. But are we hearers of the word, or doers? Do we, in pride, in shortsightedness, despise the gift we've been given, or look to live like we understand the blessing it is?

God has given us His word that we may know His will.

Whosoever cometh to me, and heareth my sayings, and doeth them, I will shew you to whom he is like: He is like a man which built an house, and digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock: and when the flood arose, the stream beat vehemently upon that house, and could not shake it: for it was founded upon a rock. But he that heareth, and doeth not, is like a man that without a foundation built an house upon the earth; against which the stream did beat vehemently, and immediately it fell; and the ruin of that house was great.

This is a promise. One we can count on, if we do it. If we live by His word, which is like a foundation of rock, we will not be moved.

If we don't, but lean into our own understanding, we are building on shifting sands. To be washed away.

Therefore let us build on that rock.

teachings.title: He that hath ears to hear, let him hear
teachings.summary: Having ears to hear means choosing to be fertile ground, doers of the word who live out the Isaiah 61 mission rather than letting cares of the world choke the seed.
teachings.text:
I would add to the points made about the parable of the sower in the other Gospels, that before explaining it to His disciples, as Jesus ended the preaching to the people who'd gathered to see Him, He cries out, "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear."

We have talked about how Jesus used parables that those seeking truth would hear, and understanding come to accept the Gospel, but those with hardened hearts were deaf to it. Unable to understand. They were like the well worn and compacted dirt of the pathway that the seed never takes to.

But if we truly have ears to hear, it isn't enough to understand the meaning of the parable. It isn't simply "getting it" but understanding it and being pricked in the heart to be that fertile ground that produces abundantly, rather than the more worldly and unfruitful Christians. Hearing should compel us to be more than just saved. To whom much is given, much is expected. We are to prepare our hearts that we be fertile, to water the growing spirit inside us with the word. To grow deep roots in scripture and to branch out higher and higher as we seek the light.

It is up to us whether we be the rock or the thorny ground, or if we are fertile soil. It's not just happenstance. It isn't just what it is. We have a choice. We can hide the light under a bushel or on the highest candlestick that others may see and be drawn in. We do that by obeying the word. Not being hearers only, but doers.

Remember, to obey is better than sacrifice. Abstinence and fasting and not sinning in a manner we aren't prone to anyway is all well and good, but it is the keeping of the law, which Jesus boiled down to Love of God shown by keeping His commandments, and loving your neighbors which is the means by which we keep them.

I keep coming back to Jesus' use of **Isaiah 61** as a mission statement for Christian life, but it is key and given us for a reason:

*The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord*.

If we seek to be fertile ground, we need to make this our mantra. Our founding principle. We who are saved have been given the gift of having the Spirit of the Lord upon us. Are we frittering it away? Hiding it under a bushel? Do we allow the cares of the world to choke it out? Do we fall away having no roots?

Do we live up to the ideal that to whom much is given, much is expected? Or, will we see it taken away, being only hearers of the word and never growing past that?

It is impossible to spend time with Jesus and not have it change you. The more we diligently seek Him, the more we are given. And the more knowledge and understanding we are given, the harder and harder it becomes to live in sin. To not love others. To be lazy in our Christian life. To be afraid. To be blown away by the wind or choked out by the thorns, the cares of this world.

Let him who has ears to hear, let him hear.

teachings.title: Seventy times seven: forgive as forgiven
teachings.summary: One who has truly received God's grace for a great debt will forgive others, and a held grudge against one sincerely asking forgiveness shows a heart that never understood grace.
teachings.text:
The apostles ask Jesus, "who is greatest in the Kingdom of Heaven?" Jesus points to a child, an innocent who oblivious to the law, and unable to offend, humble and without pride, represents those who have been brought low by the truth of the Gospel, and fearing the Father, accepting His grace, just as a child is dependent and helpless before their father.

To be converted, to repent, is to accept His will, to obey the Gospel, to accept we deserve death and humbly cry for mercy, and in His grace, the Father gives it to us, redeemed by Christ, forgiven all debt incurred by our sin.

Jesus continues this lesson when Peter asks how often should we forgive a brother. The law says 3 times, he doubles it and again and asks is 7 times enough?

Jesus replies, 70 times 7, indicating an order of magnitude greater than the letter of the law. To essentially always forgive those seeking it.

And, spinning off of this, Jesus teaches how to ask for forgiveness ourselves, and what to do if a so-called brother refuses. That we ask in private, then before witnesses, as pertaining to God's law, and then, if he refuses still, to put him out and treat him as an unregenerate sinner. A publican. A heathen. Because lack of forgiveness and grace is a sign of an unsaved heart.

He tells the parable of the unforgiven servant, who beseeching the king to be forgiven a massive debt, then refuses to release a fellow servant a relatively minor one.

This lack of grace means he didn't humbly partake in the same from the king, and undeserving, is cast into prison for torment.

And so it is for all men. The Bible says Jesus paid the debt for all men. Those who seek that forgiveness in truth and reconciliation of grace will by nature show grace upon those who have wronged them. Not perfectly, we may need reminders, we may need the presence of witnesses to our stubborn pride to see our error. But holding a grudge against one who has sincerely asked to be forgiven is evidence of pride and arrogance, and a sign one has no understanding of the humility of receiving grace from God for our own trespass.

It is a humbling feeling to know you are in the hands of the Living God, and deserve death and Hell, and yet, He forgives. The prideful cannot understand because they cannot admit to themselves their own debt. They can't receive His mercy, because they think it unfair or overcharged, or worse, doesn't exist.

To them is forgiveness denied and the full price extracted.

But we forgive as we have been forgiven. We understand that there but for the grace of God go I. Even if we sometimes need a reminder to.

And our forgiveness should be as longsuffering and loving as that which was shown to us.

If you are holding a grudge against someone, and cannot let it go, you aren't right with God. If you're truly saved, you know the feeling of grace, extended to you. Forgive.

And if you can't understand grace, and hold on to your grievance, you will find yourself before the strait gate unable to enter. Like a camel entering the eye of a needle, unable to pass.

Let go and humble yourself to God in Jesus name, and receive His grace. Amen.

teachings.title: If God forgives blasphemy, forgive petty offence
teachings.summary: Since God forgives all manner of sin and blasphemy against Himself, those under grace have no ground to withhold forgiveness over the petty squabbles of this life.
teachings.text:
One thing that just occurred to me, when thinking of the grace that God the Father and Jesus the Son extend to us. Jesus says, back in Matthew 12, that all manner of sin and blasphemy, including blasphemies against him and God the Father, shall be forgiven of men. (Blasphemies against the Holy Spirit being the only unforgivable sin in this regard. For who would blaspheme the Holy Ghost but a reprobate?)

If our creator and savior can forgive great offense directed at them, how can we not do likewise for the petty squabbles of this life? If the spirit is truly within us and we are under grace, cognizant of what we deserve and aware of the mercy that's been shown on us, how can we not forgive others?

teachings.title: Philemon and Onesimus: brokering forgiveness
teachings.summary: Paul's appeal for Onesimus models how believers should forgive one another and help make peace between brethren, remembering what Christ forgave us.
teachings.text:
An epistle to Philemon, the host of a Colossian church, Paul writes from his bonds in support of Philemon's escaped slave Onesimus (or unfaithful servant, it has been debated), is an instruction on forgiveness. How we as Christians may settle scores between brothers in Christ, if not equals in station. Being peacemakers.

Onesimus apparently fled Philemon, and wound up in Paul's camp, converted to the faith by the Apostle. Philemon, his master, already a prominent Christian in the early church.

Paul's delicate appeal to take back the servant, not only as a servant, but forgiven as a brother in Christ is a model for us to follow. He reminds the elder Christian of his debt to those ministering the Gospel which he's saved by, and asks he see it right to extend the same grace to Onesimus, who is seeking forgiveness. Paul even offers to pay whatever debt is owed, though he gets in a not-so-subtle reminder that Philemon owes even moreso, having eternal life by the word preached by Paul and his fellow laborers.

We should also make overtures to bring brethren together, to help broker peace and forgiveness. And we should use reminders of what love Jesus Christ has for us that He gave Himself for us as sacrifice, that we may suffer a little worldly loss out of love for one another.

Onesimus brought this letter and the general epistle to the Colossians from Paul in Rome, and the preservation of Philemon and the promulgation of Colossians suggests that Philemon found it in his heart to forgive him, and welcome him as a brother in Christ.

teachings.title: Not cucked: Paul's subjection and boldness
teachings.summary: Being subject to the powers, living peaceably and leaving vengeance to God is not weakness, for Paul and the apostles submitted while boldly preaching the truth even unto chains and death.
teachings.text:
I was just struck with a realization about the irony of those who call Christianity "cucked," and who attempt to discredit the writings of the Apostle Paul based on his Epistles regarding the behavior of Christians, especially relative to the powers that be. To the government. Being subject to those who have power over us, given by God. To, as much as possible, live at peace with all men. Romans 13, etc.

The irony being that Paul was subject to constant persecution, was stoned to death at one point, had to be snuck out of cities in baskets least the mobs led by Jews tear him apart, and who wrote a majority of his epistles from chains. Literally bound for preaching the word of God and the gospel of Christ crucified.

We are instructed by the Bible to not riot in the daytime or take vengeance for ourselves. To render custom to who is due custom and tribute to who is due tribute. Pastors to subject themselves to Jesus, servants to their masters, husbands to loving their wives as Christ loves His brethren, wives to be subject to their husbands and children to honor their parents. To render unto Caesar that which is Caesars. To pay our taxes and obey the laws so long as they do not contradict the authority of the Lord and His word.

To have faith that God will save us from tribulation and persecution. To allow God to exact vengeance for us. To glory in our persecution for His name's sake. This isn't being "cucked," it's literally the only way we win.

And Paul, who wrote much of this from a jail cell, under house arrest, bound to a centurion by chains 24 hours a day for the cause of Christ, saw no contradiction in any of that.

As long as you're preaching the word of God, you shouldn't worry about things like hate crime laws or censorship, or any other persecution led by the Jews. Glory in your affliction and speak the truth.

In Acts, Peter, James, Paul and others are openly condemned and set up on for vocally pointing out that the Jews were antichrists who killed Christ Jesus. Stephen was martyred for "hate speech" against the Jews.

These meek and humble servants, who turned the world upsidedown with their preaching, drew a line in the sand.

They turned the other cheek, loved their enemies, heaping coals upon the heads of those who hated them by their charity and humble conversation. Living peaceably.

But when it came to the preaching of the word and the truth of those who hate Christ, they boldly spoke out, despite threats of jail, and even unto death.

Would that we are blessed by God with so strong a faith.

teachings.title: Blessed are ye poor; rejoice when persecuted
teachings.summary: Jesus told His disciples, unlike the fickle crowds seeking healing, that the poor and hungry who follow Him are blessed and should rejoice when persecuted for His name.
teachings.text:
For those that may have missed it, this weekend we went over the first two sections of **Luke 6**, scroll up if you missed it, they are important studies on the sabbath and other ordinances of the old and new covenant, and how Jesus' prayer life can inspire us to be more diligent in prayer to ascertain God's will. Here in the last 30 verses of Luke 6, we are given a lot of red-letter preaching from Jesus, and it's all important, and much of it is self explanatory. Jesus is the truth and speaks it here without using dark sayings and parables, as He begins addressing His disciples directly.

You'll notice the section begins with the masses, the multitudes, coming to Jesus to be healed. His fame has grown, the miraculous events being even more people who seek to be made whole of their infirmities, and the "virtue flowed out" of Jesus to heal them. Again, a focus of Luke, being a physician, is the nature of Jesus as a healer.

Note what the Bible says;

*And he came down with them, and stood in the plain, and the company of his disciples, and a great multitude of people out of all Judaea and Jerusalem, and from the sea coast of Tyre and Sidon, which came to hear him, and to be healed of their diseases; And they that were vexed with unclean spirits: and they were healed. And the whole multitude sought to touch him: for there went virtue out of him, and healed them all.And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said...*

Now, to increase the reach of His ministry and to serve those He can with the multitudes coming, Jesus had prayed and appointed of His disciples 12 Apostles, ordained of the ministry He was about, finding the lost sheep of Israel. Disciples, those who followed Him to learn, many who were saved believers, some were not (Judas for example). The 12 Apostles would be joined by 70 or so more at a later point in His earthly ministry, were those qualified to be sent out, to the highways and hedges, to preach and heal in His name. These disciples had left their lives and professions behind to follow Christ. They were poor, often hungry (earlier they were gleaning a field for some corn to eat), they moved about with His ministry, walking the wastes between towns and cities. God provides, but they were sacrificing to be Jesus' students.

But the multitudes, we are told repeatedly, flocked to see Jesus that they may be healed by proximity, to take the virtue that came out of Him. To witness a miracle or to see a sign. Of these mobs, most didn't come to a saving faith, despite what they witnessed, even those affected first hand. Some did to be sure, but most didn't as we are reminded at the crucifixion where the same people who lauded the coming of the son of David with palm fans and hosannas, days later called for His blood. They were there, like many transient "Christians" today, just there for the show.

In this context, the transition here in Luke chapter 6 is interesting. The mob presses on Jesus to be healed of their ailments, but Jesus looks from His work to address directly His disciples with this sermon, and the first topic is on humility.

He says blessed are you who are poor, hungry, in tears now, because you will be inheriting the Kingdom of God, your needs will be met. This application is not only for them that followed Christ then, but a comfort to us as well, today.

And with that comfort, comes a warning. He says to His disciples that they will also receive persecution, just as the prophets did, and from the very people that surrounded them as Jesus healed. The Jews' fathers treated the prophets like criminals and often killed them for the truth they preached. In a like manner they will be persecuted, but, Jesus say "*Rejoice ye in that day, and leap for jo*y," when this happens to you. It's a blessing to be persecuted for His name's sake.

And you can sense that Jesus then begins speaking loudly, turning His voice to the crowds. Still talking to His disciples, but addressing those surrounding them:

teachings.title: Live blamelessly; be persecuted for His name
teachings.summary: Unlike partisan cries of hypocrisy, Jesus lived blamelessly so He was persecuted only for righteousness, and we must avoid sinful rage so that persecution glorifies God.
teachings.text:
One mistake many make in politics, especially among conservatives but it is widespread, is the constant screaming of "hypocrisy!" against opponents. But it is done in hypocritical manner for cheap partisan gain. It isn't sincere. And it just becomes an impotent exercise in "They are the real [bad thing they accuse us of]!"

Because both "sides" are hypocrites, they cannot effectively use the other's hypocrisy, and it just becomes empty gestures. If anything, reinforcing the hypocrisy of each side, justified by the hypocrisy of the other.

But Jesus' intentions are pure. He is doing the will of the Father. And while, yes He is blameless in a way none of us are, His example is ours to follow.

We as Christians are commanded in scripture to live blamelessly, to as much as possible live in peace with all men. To render unto Caesar. To give custom and tribute and honor to those in position to receive it, knowing we are heirs to a better country, an eternal kingdom.

Jesus showed the way, giving them nothing to accuse Him with, so that, in the end, it was His righteousness that they persecuted Him for. That it was their own wickedness that brought Him to the cross.

In a like manner we should strive to live in a way that is blameless, making our stand in the word of God. Doing His will. Calling out evil and giving the gospel to the poor. Judgment to the fatherless. Protecting the widows. Giving comfort to the brokenhearted.

And so, of tribulation comes and persecution with it, we be persecuted for His name's sake that God receives the glory.

That when they come for you, it is because of their wickedness, not your own. And joyfully receive tribulation knowing that God will repay them with wrath, and you with eternal reward.

This is a difficult thing for many, even saved Christians who have done much to sanctify themselves. There is a pride and arrogance that gives a place for wrath, and righteous anger turns to sinful rage. It allows the wicked to claim the moral high ground. It is why they tempt us constantly with degenerate culture and unjust treatment. The gaslighting and humiliation ritual. All manner of provocation, designed to get us to fall that they may accuse us, and, in their twisted view and by the judgment of this world, justify their hatred.

But their hatred is of God the Father and His judgment, Christ in His righteousness, the Holy Spirit and His conviction of sin in their hearts.

We are just the totems of their hatred of God. And by giving cause to accuse us, they bring a bad report of God's people. We aid them in justifying their hatred of God.

And so, we can choose to stand on the rock of the word and not be moved, rejoicing at the persecution that comes knowing it brings glory to God and shows the unbelieving His power, and exposing those who oppose Christ, or we can be petty and foolish and prideful that the unbelieving will see our persecution and think, "Good. They deserve it."

Pray we have the faith to do what's right that God may glory when the devil comes to tempt us.

teachings.title: The one leper who returned to give thanks
teachings.summary: All ten lepers were healed as all believers are saved, but only one returned to give thanks, a picture of the few who go beyond bare minimum Christianity.
teachings.text:
*And it came to pass, as he went to Jerusalem, that he passed through the midst of Samaria and Galilee.*

And there Jesus saw ten lepers, calling out to be healed. And as was custom under the law as we saw earlier in Luke, Jesus says they are healed, go show the priests and do the sacrifices that they may be proved clean.

And all but one go off. The remaining one, a Samaritan. By implication the others were Jews. (They might not be, but it seems the purpose of God to point this out.)

The healed Samaritan stays, falling before Jesus in thanks, praising God.

Jesus asks where the other 9 were, this stranger, a non-Jew, says they can't be found, that they were healed and took off. Jesus tells Him his faith has made him whole. Not only healed physically, but saved spiritually.

Now to those of us saved spiritually, by faith, calling out "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us" that in His grace we be forgiven, there is a lesson here.

Physical healing, a picture of our spiritual healing in salvation, we see Jesus tell them to go on their way. He doesn't ask they praise God or worship Him in thanksgiving. He heals them and says to go do what you're supposed to. In this case the ritual ordinances relating to the healing of a leper. In ours, the basics of the faith, showing we are clean as it were. Turn from sin, read your Bible, say your prayers, love God, love others.

Bare minimum Christianity.

Few, maybe one out of ten as is the example here, actually realize what a gift they've been given and rather than the bare minimum, seek to serve Him more, in praise and thanksgiving.

All ten were healed. All who believe are given eternal life. But it is the rare few who follow it up with this level of devotion as pictured by the Samaritan.

teachings.title: We are unprofitable servants: how faith grows
teachings.summary: Jesus answered how to grow faith by teaching that doing our duty only makes us unprofitable servants, so faith grows when in humble gratitude we do more.
teachings.text:
Luke's Gospel has been focused on the costs and consequence of discipleship. Of what following Christ actually means. That we are not only healed, justified by faith through the grace of God in Jesus name, but how we grow our faith that we may better serve Him in gratitude.

The disciples here ask Jesus to show them how to grow their faith. He says if they had the smallest amount of faith they could uproot a sycamine tree, and plant it in the sea. A sycamine is known for its incredibly deep and strong roots. It is not just some shallow rooted pine. Jesus uses extremes in examples to give us a measure of what He means.

But His answer as to how we grow our faith actually ties in and dovetails perfectly with the story of the 10 lepers.

Jesus says that when a servant is finished with his chores in the day, the master doesn't treat him as if he's accomplished something extra. He doesn't have him come and sit and feast. What Jesus is saying is the servant did what he's supposed to do. And that the right attitude having done that bare minimum, should be *We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.*

This is how we grow our faith. This is Jesus answer to them to this specific pointed question.

Just as the nine lepers went and did what they were told to do, what was expected of them, didn't make them remarkable. A leper healed from his incurable illness was meant to go to the priest and offer the sacrifices and perform the rituals of cleansing to prove they were healed.

I have to note it again. The order of things here, where in the leper is healed already and then they do the things required of them. (Again, understanding that this Old Testament law was put into place as a foreshadowing of what Jesus would do specifically for the purpose of these instructions in doctrine. God is great. Amen?)

Jesus says that we can grow our faith not by doing the bare minimum but realizing that doing bare minimum of what's expected of us makes us unprofitable servants. That in our realization we become as that Samaritan who, being healed, did more. Expressing his gratitude with humility.

Again, Jesus doesn't demand this of the 10 lepers when they are healed. Only that they do what they're obliged to. Just as the servant who plows the fields and then comes in and makes the meal and serves the master is doing just the bare minimum. What he's expected to do.

It is the humility and understanding the honor that we get to serve God, being unworthy and unprofitable, doing more than the bare minimum. Without expectation of praise for what is honestly the least we can do. The following of the law. Following the commandments of God. The least we can do.

And if we seek to grow our faith, realize that that is the bare minimum and strive to do more.

teachings.title: The one or the nine: bare minimum Christians
teachings.summary: We must ask whether we are like the thankful Samaritan or the nine bare minimum Christians, and not judge others when we fall short ourselves.
teachings.text:
And so, we have to ask ourselves, are we like the one Samaritan? Followers of Christ, doing more, willing to forsake everything for the ministry of the Gospel? Growing in our faith the more we realize just how great a gift we've been given, and so loving Jesus that we devote ourselves to following Him. Picking up our cross.

Or are we like the 9? Saved, for certain. Healed of our transgressions and doing the basics, following the commandments of the law, but little else. Doing what we ought to by obligation, and little else. Unprofitable servants. Bare minimum Christians.

Or worse, are we not even holding up that weak standard? Is our faith so little that we don't even do that which is expected. Falling short of that bare minimum expectation? Caring so little about our healing that we don't stop to praise God and seek to do more for Him except the basics, and failing to do even that.

This hits hard. I fall short. But it's the lesson that is being taught, and we cannot ignore it.

If you fall short of that bare minimum, or if you do your best to do what you're obligated to, and little else, don't judge others and their Christian walk. Don't be a stumbling block or a cause of offense. *Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling*.

teachings.title: We melt down the treasure God provided
teachings.summary: Like Israel turning Egypt's gold into the calf, saved Christians who forget the bondage God freed them from turn their blessings into idols and excuses to sin.
teachings.text:
I find it interesting that in spoiling Egypt, where the people gave the Israelites their gold and treasure, would ultimately become grievous sin in the wilderness, melted down to form the image of the calf the Hebrews worshipped while Moses was on Mt Sinai with God.

Is that a picture of the blessings we have as saved Christians, which by not staying with the word of the Lord, not walking in the new man with the remembrance of the bondage God freed us from in Christ, that we risk turning to sin; into idols?

How often we forget our deserved fate. How often we forget what should have happened to us based on our choices, and spared the worst of the consequences by God in His mercy through Christ Jesus.

I don't know a saved Christian, no matter how backslidden and carnal, who when pressed won't admit that God saved them physically from the most grave of consequences they rightly deserved. Moving things in our life in such a way that we were delivered from the fruit of our sin, as we gained faith. But many forget when it's not present in their mind. Many take their blessings for granted and turn their comfort into an excuse to sin.

There are people who have relatively easy lives and yet never come to peace with their life and the choices they made. And so they are miserable.

We who are saved are blessed, that we can come to terms with it and understand what a blessing things actually are when you consider how bad it could be given the choices we've made.

The humility and perspective we gain by understanding just how pitiful our position was that we trusted in God and called upon the name of the Lord, should allow us to see the bondage He freed us from and appreciate the wilderness He's led us through on our way to the promised land.

God spares us by saving us from ourselves. His hand is constantly upon us. Like the Hebrews. His light, guiding us in the darkness. His bread, His word, come down from Heaven to feed and nourish us like manna.

And like the Hebrews, we often complain at the hardships we must endure to get ourselves back to the place God has intended for us had we not sojourned in Egypt. Had we not chased after sin.

We forget where we were. We forget how we escaped. We forget how the blood of the lamb upon our hearts, as it was upon the doorposts, spared us from destruction.

We melt down the treasure God provided, and, *as it is written, The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.*

teachings.title: Lest the people repent when they see war
teachings.summary: God guides new believers away from the worst trials early, and remembering His strong arm keeps us from turning back to the bondage of Egypt, as the parable of the sower warns.
teachings.text:
And so commanded God to all of Israel. To commemorate the day He freed them from bondage and brought them out to the land He promised their fathers, and gave ordnances regarding the feast of unleavened bread, the removal of all yeast and leavening from the home for 7 days, and the consecration of the firstborn males, in remembrance of the slaying of the firstborn of Egypt and as a picture of the Christ to come.

Leaven represents sin in the Bible. Egypt, bondage to sin. This is done in remembrance of God, just as the Lord's supper took the place of Passover, and Jesus took the place of the lamb without blemish. And so going forward, Isralites were to offer sacrifice of the first born, and in place of their first born, to sacrifice them.

Jews today claim the bar mitzvah, the purchase of sanctification by use of silver shekels, is the equivalent of the blood sacrifice required by God, because they don't worship Him or follow the Old Testament at all. They worship moloch, and follow the traditions of men.

The idea of parents instilling in their firstborn male the knowledge of Him, and what He has done for Israel is important. God needed them to retain knowledge of Him and His Promises in mind throughout generations, that in the days of Jesus, a remnant may be saved.

God, with a firey pillar by night and a pillar of smoke as a cloud, by day, took the Israelites and the mixed multitudes our, towards the Red Sea, that they not pass through the land of the Philistines, *Lest peradventure the people repent when they see war, and they return to Egypt*.

We see this in newly saved Christians lives, all the time. There is an effort by God to guide us away from the worst tribulation in the beginning, that our faith grows, so we don't immediately turn back to sin. To bondage of the law.

We know from the parable of the sower that even this period of the newness of the joy of salvation isn't enough for many. That the joy and relief can give way to the cares of the world.

*Some fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth: and forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth: And when the sun was up, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away. And some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprung up, and choked them.*

Not everyone who is saved is fertile ground. Many fall away or become offended by and by. That is why the Apostles were so intent on edification. On walking in the new man.

Even David, the apple of God's eye, felt this:

**Psalm 51:12-14**
*Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation; and uphold me with thy free spirit.Then will I teach transgressors thy ways; and sinners shall be converted unto thee. Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, thou God of my salvation: and my tongue shall sing aloud of thy righteousness.*

But by keeping in memory the strong arm of the Lord that has lifted us out of bondage by His own works, by the atonement and sanctification given us by Christ's blood, His death burial and resurrection, we will not repent towards Egypt, but press on to the promised land.

teachings.title: Who is on the Lord's side
teachings.summary: At the golden calf some never truly believed, some like Aaron backslid, and a remnant stood with God, so we should not be cocky but fear God's scourging of His sons.
teachings.text:
But, again we see the parallels to spiritual salvation, and the application of these things that serve as our examples. That many when led up out of bondage to sin and to the wilderness that is our earthly life, fall away having believed in vain. Never truly having faith. Turning immediately to other gods and to sin. Others, like Aaron, who have faith and accepted God's grace, backslide and go with the crowd, falling into sin. Still others like the sons of Levi, stand back, a loyal remnant of God.

Like the parable of the sower, there are some seeds sown that never take root, others that have shallow roots but are taken away by the cares of the world. And some falls on fertile ground and with deep roots produces much fruit.

It is easy to look at the Isralites, throughout the Old Testament, as a uniquely wicked and ungrateful people, who don't love the Lord, their deliverer, as they should.

But we shouldn't get too cocky in our own conceits. Because none of us live up to what we should. All of us fall short and with a stiff neck of our own will, stand in defiance of the Lord who bought us, putting our own will before His. Christians today who sit down to eat and drink and rise up to play.

We should consider the fate of those 3,000. God will scourge every son He receives.

It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the Living God.

teachings.title: Bless them which persecute you
teachings.summary: Be generous and hospitable and bless persecutors, trusting God to repay and to crush our enemies, which is pure religion.
teachings.text:
*Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality. Bless them which persecute you: bless, and curse not. Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.*

We see the simplicity of this love, repeated throughout the New Testament. Be generous. Charitable. Merciful. Hospitable.

Bless them that curse you. Turn the other cheek. Trust in God to repay, for vengeance is His. As Jesus says in **Matthew 5**:

*And if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloke also. And whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain. Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away.*

Don't let your pride, covetousness, wrath and offense at the inequities of the ungodly be a snare for your carnal mind. God has you. And if you suffer loss for Him, He will repay with rewards greater than you can imagine, and crush our enemies for His sake under His heel. This is the promise of the Gospel, as much as our redemption and eternal life. Every knee shall bow. We will rule and reign with Christ, and He has a rod of iron to correct the ungodly.

Better we practice our faith, our religion that is, with this in mind.

**James 1:27**
*Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.*

As I pointed out during our study of Luke, Jesus gives us a mission statement to live by:

*The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord.*

Amen!

teachings.title: As much as lieth in you, live peaceably
teachings.summary: Walking in the Spirit makes us generous, patient, just and peaceable and leaves vengeance to God, which is the fulfilling of the law.
teachings.text:
*Recompense to no man evil for evil. Provide things honest in the sight of all men. If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.*

You can see the theme building. And it reflects everything that Jesus taught in his earthly ministry. It is the serious implication for our faith. Love one another. Love your neighbor as yourself. It's the whole of the law.

And you'll note also, as this list of commands given us goes on, The harder and harder it is for the carnal mind to accept. That is, when you walk in the spirit you understand these things and you're less likely to be brought into a snare of wrath or greed or dishonesty and corruption, manipulating others.

Because you grow in faith in the certainty of your hope. Because you see God working in your life and all around you. His work revealed to us from the heavens in His wrath and in His love.

We live faith to faith. Not just in that we bring others to belief, but that our faith grows. As it is written, the just shall live by faith.

You're hospitable and generous to others because you know God gave you what you have and He'll provide again.

Your patient and long-suffering with others because you know He was patient in long suffering with you. When you didn't deserve it.

You are just in your judgments and fair and honest in your dealings because God was just in His judgment and merciful to you, in truth.

And you don't seek vengeance because you know that that belongs to God. And you know that He is not slack when it comes to delivering just punishment on the wicked. Just as Sodom and Gomorrah are held up for an example.

And so as much as possible, an important caveat that will cover more extensively in chapter 13, but as much as possible, we live peaceably with all men.

This is the implication of our faith, and the understanding of our hope, and a meek and humble acknowledgment of our condition. To better be servants of God.

teachings.title: Heap coals of fire on his head
teachings.summary: Doing good to enemies is strength, not weakness: it often turns enemies into friends, and it frustrates the wicked while God repays.
teachings.text:
*Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.*

*Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head. Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.*

And so just finishing up the chapter. We see that this doesn't just apply to brethren, It doesn't just apply to our neighbors, but it really does apply to our enemies as well. But not in the sense our detractors claim; the weakness that they perceive from this.

But in truth. Its strength.

Again, I'm going to cover this more tomorrow God willing. But we see that in our faith there is understanding of the nature of God. That He will repay. And in our well-doing, in our charity to those who persecute us, curse us, and who do evil to us, we heap hot coals upon their head.

It enrages the truly wicked when we show, by our faith, kindness towards them in need. When we turn the other cheek.

For those that aren't necessarily wicked but worldly, this provides an opportunity for them to see the love of God through us and wins many of them over. 9 times out of 10 when someone offends you and you turn the other cheek and offer it to them, which isn't an act of submission but of defiance, you will see that most people back down. Where they may have struck an anger, literally or metaphorically, they will be made to feel ashamed. It humbles them and often brings about peace. Making an enemy into a friend.

But knowing the wicked, that it frustrates them being that they are implacable and unmerciful and full of all unrighteousness, we can take comfort in the fact that by our defiant and cheerful service to the gospel, by our faith in the Lord to repay with vengeance that is His, they are made more miserable. And God given more glory.

They will be punished in this world and the next. While we will have an eternity with God and His love.

teachings.title: Do we live so our loved ones would follow
teachings.summary: With family and friends rejecting the gospel, believers should ask whether their fearless, grateful, Bible-reading, gospel-preaching lives would draw others to Christ.
teachings.text:
This is a powerful and sobering thought. Knowing your dad or mom, sister or brother, son or daughter, reject the Gospel and on the road to reprobation, or who are trapped in their zeal without knowledge, working their way to Hell by not obeying the Gospel.

We know God is perfectly just. We know in His love we are saved, undeserved, entirely by grace, because we have believed the report. But do we live in a way that these people who we care about can emulate? Would they want to? What advantage do they see in accepting salvation, in how you live?

Are you fearful? Do you stress from the news of the world, the fake and gay theater the beast system presents to keep the cattle in pens for slaughter?

Do you live in gratitude and prayer to God in Jesus name?

Do you read your Bible and go to church? Do you boldly proclaim the Gospel to every creature, giving a ready and meek answer to the lively hope you have in Christ?

teachings.title: An example of the believers
teachings.summary: When loved ones are perishing, believers should stay steadfast and peaceful as an example, since no one will believe our hope if we are as fearful as everyone else.
teachings.text:
A common lament of the believer is that their friends and family are perishing, damned without faith. The worry and stress of having that knowledge and their inability to convince them of the truth leaves many feeling impotent and frustrated. But this is all the more reason to remain steadfast. To magnify God's love for us, reflecting it to those we care about. To be the rock that they can turn to when they are troubled, and maybe coming to see the truth of the word though our example. The reason for our hope. To be *an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.*

Why would someone believe someone telling them of the peace that passes all understanding found in Christ when we are as miserable and fearful as everyone else?

teachings.title: Not peace, but a sword
teachings.summary: The gospel brings division even in our families, and loving Christ above parents and children means taking up the cross and bearing their hatred for His name.
teachings.text:
Jesus continues His instructions, telling them that God is watching over them, and what we preach, fearlessly from the rooftops as it were, may bring condemnation by men, division within even our own families.

The peace of God given by His Son to those that believe will not bring peace on earth between men. They will hate us for His name's sake. Those that accuse Jesus of being Beelzebub will accuse us likewise. If you have been born again for any length of time, you have experienced this. Especially within family. Those that know us best and who refuse the truth, resent and turn on us, accusing our every deed, hating us for His grace within us. Our sins thrown against us, and lies used to accuse.

That's why Jesus says if we love our parents or siblings or children more than Him, we aren't worthy. We must carry the cross, despising the shame, just as He did. Not caring for our very life, willing to die for God's will, just as Jesus did.

teachings.title: Whosoever will lose his life for my sake
teachings.summary: Believers should take up the cross willing to die for Christ, because our blessed hope is eternal life and reward at His coming in glory.
teachings.text:
Jesus again admonishes those of his disciples who sought for him to avoid earthly persecution, which they in turn would receive for their faith, to not be afraid to pick up their cross and follow him. To be willing to be crucified and like manner, laying down their earthly life, because we have eternal life as our reward:

*For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it. For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul? For the Son of man shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.*
*Verily I say unto you, There be some standing here, which shall not taste of death, till they see the Son of man coming in his kingdom.*

This is our hope as believers, this is our blessed assurance. We'll not taste of death, but rather we will live to see the son of man coming into his glory, and the coming of the Kingdom of Heaven. Our flesh may parish but our spirit has eternal life and our glorified bodies will be risen on that day, and our works for Him will be weighed and rewarded. Amen.

And so, with this promise, we shouldn't care for our life in this world. We should take up our cross willing to die for Him, just as He was for us.

teachings.title: The first shall be last: humility in service
teachings.summary: The parable of the labourers rebukes pride and striving over who is greatest; entrance to the Kingdom is the reward, and service done in childlike humility is greater than works done in contention.
teachings.text:
The Gospels shows that even among Christ's staunchest followers, there was competition between some of the Apostles. Who will be greater in the Kingdom of Heaven? What reward will they receive for their devotion? Even John telling of the footrace he won with Peter to Christ's empty tomb. This continued even after the day of Pentecost, and the contentions between Peter and Paul.

These human traits of pride and expectation are laid bare by God in His word, just as the great men of the OT, patriarchs, prophets and kings, are all shown to be flawed humans. Prone to sin. Often prideful. Sometimes foolish. The Apostles are no different, and suffer more for comparison to Jesus, who is perfect, the only truly perfect man in scripture, being God in the flesh.

It is fascinating from a literary sense, how consistently and fully fleshed out most of those who appear in the Bible are, as characters. And the spiritual aspect, a constant reminder of who we are, and who God uses for His purposes on Earth.

It is encouraging and yet humbling that these great men and women, human, do mighty works and yet are as weak as we are. Great in faith, but with moments of doubt. Great in the spirit of righteousness, but still sinners and weak in the flesh. Serving as examples, like Peter often does, with his well intentioned rock-headedness.

In chapter 18, they asked who would be greatest in the Kingdom, to which Jesus used a humble child to illustrate the humility that it would require.

A similar dispute occurs both in Luke 9 and Luke 22, where the Apostles are said to have had *strife among them, which of them should be accounted the greatest.*

Here, in Matthew 20, is the direct continuation of the end of 19, where Jesus had just illustrated the problem with the self-righteous and rich with humbling themselves sufficiently to enter into the Kingdom of Heaven, unable to accept the simple salvation of faith, and unwilling to give up everything in this life, for the eternal.

Peter had asked what will their reward be, having done just that. Walking away from their profession, their income, their families, wives and children to follow Jesus. And Jesus taught them they have their reward, but cautions them to remember the lesson of humility, suffering the children, and many that are first shall be last in His kingdom.

And so we are here in Matthew 20, and Jesus tells His disciples a parable. Of a man, hiring hands for the harvest, where each is given the agreed upon wage, a penny for a day's work. Those that labored from the start, and even those who labored but a short time. And the longest among them grumbled that they should receive the same reward.

But entrance to the Kingdom of Heaven is the reward itself, agreed upon in faith, and contentions of who will be greatest therein is up to the judgment of God the Father, and our own judgment of our own works does not give us the right to question this.

Believing Jews in the newly forming churches saw themselves as "first," the Gentiles, "last." Often prideful and puffed-up Christians, having been born to believers and raised in a church will look down on babes in Christ, coming from a sinful past and yet to get right in all things.

Those who volunteer at church, and attend 3 times a week. Who carry all the chairs and make the largest pot luck. Who show for soul winning times, and go on mission trips, spreading the Gospel, but not out of humility of being a servant. Not out of satisfaction of being least, and thus, doing all things from that meek humility of the recognition of their retched state, but instead out of striving and contention. Pride.

Good works done, and some reward had, for certain, when the fire burns away the wood, hay and stubble, some diamonds will surely remain. But yet, how much the greater their reward if they had become like unto children? Had been ministers to others. Willing and happy servants?

This is the lesson Jesus tries to teach His disciples, and was preparing them to see Him live out, in Jerusalem.

teachings.title: Whosoever will be chief, let him be servant
teachings.summary: In Christ's kingdom greatness is servanthood, so believers are to be meek ministers to others, accepting division and tribulation for His name.
teachings.text:
Now this exchange causes the other 10 to strive with the 2 brothers. Jesus pleas with them to not engage in that kind of dispute over who is greater.

He says that the princes of this world exercise authority by who is greater, who has the most, commands the most. But that in His kingdom it isn't so.

"*Whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant: Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many*."

This still applies today. Jesus did not come here to bring peace, but division. Separation. Among family. Among friends. From wealth and personal comfort. That we will see tribulations and persecution. And to be hated by man for His name.

The promise is that *every one that hath forsaken houses, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name's sake, shall receive an hundredfold.* That tribulation in this world is glory in the next. That being meek, poor in spirit, but great in faith, willing to suffer that others may gain, is how we are to live, and great is the reward for those of us who may.

To be servants. To wash the feet of others. To be ministers. Not puffed up. But as like unto a child. To show mercy for others, not being proud of our own righteousness but a reflection of Christ's.

And as they pass two blind beggars, persistent in their faith, Jesus has mercy upon them, and they are given their sight.

The blind made to see.

If you, like I, struggle occasionally on this lesson, how to be humble. How not to resent our status, position, wealth and comfort. How to live for Christ as a minister to the weak, with no expectations for added reward, but happy with the gift of eternal life we have hope on, listening to the Spirit with the new man inside, pray. Pray and worship, persistently. Asking Jesus to be able to see.

teachings.title: Avoid vain babblings and science falsely so called
teachings.summary: The rich are to give freely, and believers entrusted with the gospel should avoid vain disputations with scorners and heretics, which are a bad witness.
teachings.text:
Finishing up, Paul advises that Timothy lay charge to those who are converted to the faith and already rich in wealth to be ready to hand it out to those in need. To do good works with that they've been blessed. To despise their riches here and store up rewards for Heaven.

As Jesus told His disciples, it is harder for a rich man to enter the Kingdom than for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle. And because to whom much is given, much more is expected, they should be encouraged to do as much as possible for the brethren, edifying the church and giving glory to God.

Finally, Paul warns young Timothy, his son in Christ, a ward of the Gospel, to

*Keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called: Which some professing have erred concerning the faith.*

We are entrusted with the Gospel of reconciliation. The doctrines of how to live, discipleship, prudence, fidelity to God's law and hope in His promise. To preach and to teach this to every creature. Saving who we can, by mercy or by warning of the fire.

We should give good witness to this faith that we have been entrusted, the surety of which is our now quickened spirit, and the indwelling of the Holy Spirit inside us. A ready and meek answer for our hope to all who we give witness.

We are to avoid the vain, that is unprofitable babblings of those seeking to debate us, to engender strife and disputations of the faith. Not to give answer to fools. Not to get into arguments with gnostics, and their science, falsely so-called. This includes debating atheists on creation, for example. We are warned repeatedly against answering a fool in their folly.

**Proverbs 9**

*7 He that reproveth a scorner getteth to himself shame: and he that rebuketh a wicked man getteth himself a blot.*

*8 Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee: rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee.*

*9 Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning.*

It is a bad witness to get caught up in disputations with a heretic. (Of this, I am chief)

**Titus 3:10-11**
*A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject; Knowing that he that is such is subverted, and sinneth, being condemned of himself.*

(This is primarily the reason for my pinned rules for the channel. To keep myself from sinning, being drawn into debates with fools. It's also why Twitter is such a snare.)

teachings.title: Reject a heretic after two admonitions
teachings.summary: Strivings about the law and genealogies are vain, so after a heretic is shown scripture twice we should reject him rather than argue from pride.
teachings.text:
And, once again, God repeats for emphasis that we should avoid foolish questions, Jewish fables, endless genealogies, and strivings about the law; *for they are unprofitable and vain*.

Debates and silly theological questions and talmudic arguments about the law help no one. They can lead to heresy and blasphemy. They can be a snare and a stumbling block to those seeking truth. Be determined to know nothing but Christ and Him crucified.

As far as those who endlessly strive about these things? They are heretics.

*A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject.*

If you've shown them clear scripture, two times, and they still insist they are right, then shake the dust. It's not worth it to answer a fool in his folly. It's why I have the pinned rules in my chat. Sincerely asked questions, met with polite consideration when answered is one thing, but demands to go back and forth with their natural man idea of scripture is vanity. Useless. Helping no one, and may give you cause to sin and them to accuse.

*Knowing that he that is such is subverted, and sinneth, being condemned of himself* be satisfied, instead of having to prove them wrong. That's your pride, and it helps no one. (I have fallen in to this trap. It's so tempting)

Grace be with you all. Amen.

teachings.title: Meekness as strength against enemies
teachings.summary: Like Jesus silencing His tempters, believers should answer enemies with blamelessness and scripture rather than railing, letting their own hypocrisy expose them.
teachings.text:
Finally we see the murderous Jews attempting to tempt Jesus into saying something they may use to justify His death, and once again, Jesus silences them by their own hypocrisy.

This is the proper way to deal with such matters. Not reacting and railing, but trusting in God, being blameless and allowing their own internal contradictions and corruption to hamstring your enemies. Using scripture when needed. Forcing them to persecute you directly for His name's sake and for the word.

When we spiral in anger and get drawn into debate, all we do is give them the hook to hang us with. Instead, Jesus shows us how petty and foolish they are, exposing them.

This lesson in meekness as strength is often lost by believers. It's good to be constantly reminded of throughout the Gospels.

teachings.title: Correct false teachers with love from scripture
teachings.summary: Instead of striving in debates, believers should meekly correct error from the misused scripture and pray for those zealous without knowledge, since faith comes by hearing the word.
teachings.text:
Now it's important to note a few lessons for us, when we interact with unsaved people offering up false doctrines and using out of context scripture as "proof text."

This is a lesson it took me a while to learn, because we are trained in this era of social media to engage in an argument, to prove our side and own the other side. To enter into striving and debates about the law, answering foolish questions and other things that the scripture explicitly tells us not to do. It often leads to wrath, and wrath to sin. It's why the Bible tells us not to do it.
